speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 34(1), I have the honour to present to the House, in both official languages, the report of the Canada-Europe Parliamentary Association attending the visit to Yugoslavia and Bulgaria, March 14 to March 26.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a moment to add, on behalf of my colleagues in the House of Commons who were on that visit, the recommendation that the Canadian government urge the use of United Nations mediation facilities in Yugoslavia, through the good offices of the Secretary General, should the need arise.
We see this as a vital element in ensuring a peaceful, democratic future for all of Yugoslavia, whatever political choices are made.
The opportunities are great for Canada in terms of assisting both Bulgaria and Yugoslavia with their economic and democratic plights. We urge the opening of an embassy in Bulgaria, with a strong trade presence immediately, to press on as partners in the western industrialized nations the need to focus on the plight of the Bulgarian economy as it struggles to restructure. We urge to direct our trade and other officials to give a high priority to assistance, especially in the agricultural sector, to Bulgaria.
We want to alert our trade officials here in Canada to tell Canadian companies that Yugoslavia is virtually a free market and that there are tremendous opportunities for Canadians in hydro engineering and telecommunications.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and indeed a privilege to present a petition on behalf of constituents from all the communities in the North Thompson Valley of British Columbia, including Blue River, Clear Water, Barrie and Little Fort as well as Logan Lake, Chase, Westwold, Monte Creek, Monte Lake, Red Lake, Pritchard, Savona and the great city of Kamloops.
These constituents are concerned that the government has cut back on funding for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police resulting in a major loss to the province of British Columbia.
The petitioners point out that the consequences of these cuts have been the reduction and erosion of police service, effectiveness and protection. They also say that the results of these cuts have been the reduction of training, patrols and travelling expenses for the RCMP serving our communities.
The petitioners point out that the federal government is uncompromising in its negotiations with its provincial counterparts by maintaining that their share of funding will be reduced as of March 31, 1991, resulting in taxpayers having to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars more in most communities in British Columbia, to say nothing of the reduction in police protection.
The petitioners are urging the Government of Canada to consider restoring proper funding to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police so that it can fulfil its mandate and role as the only visible police force for communities across B.C. and so that it may remain a viable symbol of Canadian unity.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other colleagues I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak today on the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne which took place at the opening of the Third Session of the thirty-fourth Parliament.
I am not one who speaks often in the House, being convinced and persuaded that repeating what has already been said many times before is perhaps a waste of time.

May 16, 1991
The Address
I feel that in this Speech from the Throne there is a particular paragraph in which I think has not been duly recognized by many people, certainly not by the media. I would like to participate largely for that reason.
I would like to congratulate my two colleagues, one from St. Maurice and the other from Regina-Wascana, who moved and seconded the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Each did this in a most eloquent fashion and should be commended.
We should also note that one is a francophone from Quebec and the other an anglophone from Saskatchewan. I think we should not overlook the fact that it is possible in this country for people who have goodwill and who are willing to look at the issues in an objective way to come together and talk and act for the benefit of this country as a whole.
That was the main raison d'etre or the main issue raised in this Speech from the Throne; the one we are debating at the present time.
There were three main headings or general topics that constituted the Speech from the Throne on this particular occasion.
The first was the issue and subject of Canadian unity. The second was that of "Participating in Prosperity" and the third was "Changing the Way in which Ottawa Works". I would like to address all three of those to a greater or lesser degree, but from the somewhat unique position as a member and chairman of the previous Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons. As you know, the committees have all been dissolved with the prorogation of Parliament earlier this week, and we now await these committees being re-established. But I would like to speak from the perspective of having served on that committee and more recently as chairman for a number of years.
In the course of doing this, I want to look at the Speech from the Throne and view it in a number of ways, but particularly in how it addresses a large segment of the people of Canada, namely those who are disabled. I should inform colleagues in the House that that represents about 13 per cent of Canadians. There are many of us, of course, who feel fine and are fit at the present time. But most of us, sooner or later, are going to be subjected to being included in that group of 13 per cent
that are disabled. I think we should, for that reason, give this further consideration and perhaps more than it has had over the course of the years.
I am pleased to see that my colleague and former chairman of the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons, the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore, speaking earlier in this debate, made reference to a very important paragraph in the Speech from the Throne that I want to deal with as well. That interesting paragraph comes under the heading of "Participating in Prosperity". When one takes a cursory look at the Speech from the Throne, one might wonder indeed how a few of the three or four social issues that are mentioned, would come under that rubric or under that heading of "Participating in Prosperity", but in fact they do.
I would like at this point to quote from the Speech from the Throne the particular paragraph that I am referring to, because as I said earlier not much mention has been made of this in the last several days. I am quoting now.
My government will lay before you proposals for programs and policies to remove the barriers still faced by disabled Canadians to full participation in Canada's political life and economic prosperity. The government plans to implement a five-year strategy that will resolve issues such as access to employment, training, housing and transportation, public sensitivity and community integration.
As I mentioned earlier, I do regret the fact that there has been relatively little attention paid to this in some newspaper stories, other than where they list a series of headings from the Speech from the Throne. We do see mention of this reference to disabled people, but it is not picked up as a news item or as a story or something that somebody in the journalistic field wants to talk about or elaborate on. Virtually the same is true here in the House of Commons. I would suggest we will hear very little about this. We will hear a lot about the national unity issue and the economic problems that we are having, the need for prosperity, but perhaps not very much about this subject of the disabled and how they relate to the over-all picture.
I am not sure why that situation prevails. I might suggest that possibly the subject of disabled people is not sufficiently controversial although if you are a disabled person you might not quite agree with that. It may be that the people who are looking and writing about the
May 16, 1991

Speech from the Throne do not really realize the significance of this particular paragraph.
It is obvious to everyone that the speech does address the two main issues that I have alluded to, namely the national unity issue and the issue of the economy or the future prosperity of this country. It does this in an interesting way. It links the two issues together and shows how the one is essential for the success of the other. I think we are seeing a lot written about that now, and that is indeed appropriate.
I think that while disability might be considered a social issue by most people, as I have indicated earlier, a little thought about the subject would suggest to one that it has its own significance regarding the headings of unity and prosperity.
There is a connotation in this paragraph that the issue of the problems faced by disabled people relates to the subject of unity and also relates to the over-all picture of the economy and prosperity in this country. I will want to elaborate on that before I finish.
Before doing that, I also want to quote another short paragraph from the Speech from the Throne. It appears in the first introductory page of the speech, before we launch into the specifics of unity. There are a number of words in it I want to touch on as being particularly significant in several ways. The paragraph reads as follows:
This session will be a turning point in Canadian history.
It is going to be a turning point, but it is a turning point for those who are disabled as well. For the first time, we find a confirmation and a commitment by the government that it is now going to have a five year strategy to deal with the needs, the problems of access and so on of disabled people.
While it may be a turning point in general for Canadians and for Canada, it is also a turning point, I would submit, for disabled people. The paragraph continues:
Let no one doubt the seriousness of the challenges we face as a
country.
If any group in this country faces a challenge it is the disabled community. They have been recognized as being disabled. They have, in the past, been set aside and overlooked. We are now seeing an attempt made by government and by the committee of this House to
The Address
address those challenges that they are facing and try to help them to overcome them.
The paragraph goes on to say:
You will have the responsibility and the opportunity to forge an
historic accommodation that embraces all Canadians,-
We do, indeed, have a responsibility. I would submit we also have an opportunity now, through this Speech from the Throne, to do exactly that, to make this historic accommodation.
The word "accommodation" brings to mind a couple of points. First of all, if we are going to have national unity in this country, various groups have to learn to better accommodate one another. I would also submit that it raises in the minds of those of us involved with disabled people the fact that they are looking and seeking for the term which is referred to as "reasonable accommodation", added to the Canadian Human Rights Act. At the present time, there is no requirement for employers, for example, to supply reasonable accommodation for disabled people. I was pleased to see this very word used in the Speech from the Throne and, of course, as it says here, it has to embrace all Canadians. For a change, we can assume then that among all these Canadians will be those who are disabled.
The throne speech goes on to say:
-overcomes division and discord and charts a course for
prosperity for generations to come.
Indeed, we are looking at prosperity not only for those of us who are able-bodied Canadians, but also prosperity for those who are disabled because they form part of the over-all picture of all Canadians.
I am pleased that we can see that kind of wording in the Speech from the Throne and we should compliment the government for taking that position.
The Speech from the Throne serves to focus, as I have suggested previously, on the bonds and the ties between the subject areas of unity and prosperity and how one is necessary for the other. That makes a great deal of sense and I am sure much has and will be said about that in the course of this debate.
The speech goes on, under the heading of "Participating in Prosperity", to address the need to consider, in addition to disabled people, other social issues as well. I just want to acknowledge the fact that it does indicate the need to address the issue of education, the role and needs of aboriginal peoples in this country and the issue of children. This arises, to some extent, from the

May 16, 1991
The Address
considerable involvement that Canada had, through the Prime Minister playing a leading role at the UN conference on children last fall.
There are other social issues, but I want to, by and large, confine my remarks to the one dealing with the disabled people. Like the issue of disabled people, these areas that I have alluded to relate closely to economic prosperity and unity issues. They also transcend the traditional controversial and divisive issues of language, culture and so on.
At this point it would be appropriate to indicate that the work of the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons is the type of work that transcends some of the divisive areas we have in this country. For example, discussions are taking place whereby the committee will plan to visit Quebec and look at the problems disabled people have there. That is helping to bridge a gap between the two language issues within this country.
We also have in mind, after having done it 10 years ago, a visit to the native peoples of Canada and try to understand better their needs vis-a-vis disabled persons, but by doing so we are also bridging gaps that lie between the aboriginal people at the present time and the rest of us in this country.
The history of the standing committee that I alluded to is interesting. I would like just to comment a little bit on that committee and the work that it has done in the past. Before I do that, I want also to acknowledge the fact that the third item that we are dealing with in the Speech from the Throne, namely the changing of the way Ottawa works, is also well exhibited in what the standing committee has been able to do over the last 10 years and even prior to when it became actually a standing committee.
It shows how this issue of unity can be seen to work on Parliament Hill among political parties, and a brief resume of some of the work of the committee will illustrate that.
Those hon. members who have been around for a while will recall that the late Hon. Walter Dinsdale was probably the first and the main champion of disabled people in this country. He proposed for a number of years that there should be a study made of the needs of
disabled people. Finally, in 1979, during the Clark government, agreement was reached to have such a committee established, but that government fell before the committee could be set up. The defeat led to a change in government, but not a change in the desire to have this committee move ahead. Under the Trudeau government at that time, the Special Committee on Disabled and Handicapped People was struck, chaired by David Smith, at that time an MP from Toronto.
Mr. Smith fashioned a very excellent, non-partisan committee. The style of functioning was essentially non-partisan which led to the committee being able to come up with the unanimous report entitled "Obstacles". It was so well that received it went through three printings because of the demand for it.
I cannot help but mention, again alluding to the issue of unity, the fact that the only surviving member of the House now of that original committee is the hon. member for Beaches-Woodbine. I want to acknowledge the fact that he has been a prime example of how we can work together as members of a committee in a non-partisan fashion for the good of the people of Canada, in this particular case, for the good of those who are disabled.
I just want to acknowledge that fact because I think altogether too often we find partisanship prevailing. In my view, the people of Canada are becoming a little tired of that, but there are examples in this House where that does not have to happen.
The committee went on after having presented its report on "Obstacles" to go through many other changes and has presented many other reports over the years. I want to allude to the fact that in 1985 it became a subcommittee and was under the chairmanship of the member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore. That committee made several reports.
One of the interesting things that happened in 1987 was the acceptance by the Speaker of the House of Commons, who decided it was appropriate to establish a task force on disabled and handicapped on Parliament Hill. He came up with a very voluminous report indicating the changes that needed to take place on the Hill and set an example for government departments and agencies to do more themselves on behalf of the people of
May 16, 1991

Canada. I am proud to think that our Speaker was able to take the lead in that regard.
Following that, in 1988, the committee assumed the full status of a standing committee and since then is known as the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons. It is interesting to look at the terms of reference of the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons. They are unique terms of references. No other committee has precisely these terms. I say this in reference to the changing patterns of work here on the Hill.
Reading from the Standing Orders of the House of Commons of May 1991, page 75, Item 108(3)(b)(ii), the terms of reference state:
(ii) the proposing, promoting, monitoring and assessing of initiatives aimed at the integration and equality of disabled persons in all sectors of Canadian society;
We have that unique opportunity of proposing, promoting, monitoring and assessing. I want to suggest that it has given the committee an opportunity which has not always existed in the past and it does suggest a move to make the standing committees and the ordinary members of Parliament much more effective.
The other thing that has happened because of the ability of the committee to propose and to monitor and to be advocates on behalf of disabled people, is the fact that we shall be entering the fourth National Access Awareness Week two weeks from this week. I would like to pay tribute to the fact that this has been something that has been accomplished over the last four years by a collaborative effort by a number of groups in this country including the Federation of Canadian Municipalities that have combined with others to produce the Five Star Community Awards that are presented during National Access Awareness Week. These include about ten of the leading companies in Canada. I will not read them all because of the shortage of time.
I see my time is running out. I want to remind members that two weeks from yesterday, this fourth National Access Awareness Week is going to be held here in Canada and we are going to recognize that on the Hill when the standing committee is going to co-host,
The Address
along with the Speaker of the House of Commons, a reception in the Railway Committee Room, to which I hope all will attend. At that particular reception we will be bringing to the attention of members Independence '92, which is going to be taking place in Vancouver next year and will represent the culmination of the UN Decade of the Disabled.
I would like to say a lot more about this subject. I know my time is up and I will reserve further comments until a later date.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a parliamentarian and a Quebecer, I was very disappointed by the Speech from the Throne.
Instead of a global vision of our country, I heard only words devoid of logic, rhetoric devoid of substance. Instead of finding substance, especially in the kind of action to be taken by the government, I heard only promises. Not promises for today, Mr. Speaker, not promises for tomorrow, but promises for the year 2000.1 find that incredible.
Instead of showing sensitivity in the Speech from the Throne- we must understand that what Canadians are looking for in this Speech is whether the government is aware of the problems of the unemployed, of women who want daycare, of consumers who are seeking better protection, and workers who are seeking better protection as well. These people want a government that is sensitive to their problems, and instead, all the government does is urge us to be more competitive.
To be competitive, however, means that as a worker you are well paid. It means that as a trucker-like our truckers outside-you are competing on a level playing field. But that is not the case.
The government wants all Canadians and Quebecers to be more competitive. Exactly what does that mean? I think it means the government wants us to take a cut in pay and work more.
I wonder, however, how cutting people's pay and making them work longer hours is going to make us more competitive. I know that the people in my riding, don't agree. In my riding, people say that the work they do is not a problem, because in Quebec people have always been productive. That is not the problem.

May 16, 1991
The Address
The reason we are not competitive enough-and I quote the Wall Street Journal, which is probably the Tory government's bible-is the way we manage the Canadian economy. In fact, the former Minister of Finance-I haven't heard any more about this but it's true-was called the worst Minister of Finance of any of the world's developed countries. And that is saying a lot! The worst in the world, and this from the Wall Street Journal! In Canada, we know how to do things. We know how to distinguish ourselves. Just look at the former Minister of Finance who was called the world's worst Finance minister!
When we talk about-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I see members on the other side are wide awake. They aren't late this morning. They are bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. That's good.
When we talk about the hypocrisy and lack of truthfulness of this government, I have yet to hear the government say: Sure, we made mistakes; sure, we lied to you about the GST; we misled you about tax reform. I have not heard them say anything of the kind. Instead of admitting his mistakes, the Prime Minister used the Speech from the Throne to brag: I did not make any mistakes, and I made some difficult decisions. Good grief, they were not difficult decisions, they were the wrong decisions! That is why he got this slap in the face from the Wall Street Journal, because the government has been making the wrong decisions about the economy for the past six years.
I realize my conservative colleagues are upset because I am blaming them. I agree they cannot be expected to take all the blame, because in 1984 they inherited an incredible deficit which was the result of the incompetence and arrogance of the former Liberal government. I remember. I realize that is how it all started. But as angered as I was by what happened under the previous government, it is totally unrelated to what is happening now under this government. The Liberal arrogance and incompetence has been replaced by a corporate agenda calling for the Conservatives to do certain things to please our friends the banks and big businesses. That is what we got for trying to boost our economy somewhat when we were deep into a "made in Canada" recession. Again, Canada has the know how. This government surely knows how to plunge us deep into a recession.
There is more, Mr. Speaker. After plunging us into a deep and severe recession, the government has the gall to blame us Canadians for contributing to this recession. How is that?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is the Tory way!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
True. That is the Toiy way of doing things. They blamed us for this recession. They said that we do not work enough, that we are greedy and spoiled. Quite frankly, it takes a lot of gall to say something like that!
Now, we are facing three national problems requiring direct and immediate action. These are, unemployment, unfair taxation and national unity.

This government's corporate agenda of high interest rates, high taxes and a high Canadian dollar has put millions of Canadians out of work. Free trade and unemployment insurance cuts together ensure that these jobs will never return and that the government's safety net for the jobless has wider gaps than ever.
If you do not believe there are gaps, come to my riding of Chambly and listen to people who have had to sell their homes because they lost their jobs, who had to move out of their community, who have to shop across the border. The government is making us nomadic shoppers, driving us away from our own country with its own taxation policies. Go to your ridings and listen to the people.
Montreal, Quebec, my own home town, has 12.5 per cent unemployment, the highest unemployment in Canada. That is my town and this is my country. I do not believe that the one-third of the caucus who are from Quebec can say they defend Quebec's interests while allowing 12.5 per cent unemployment to continue. That is not defending Quebec's interests.
Allow me to speak on the second national crisis we are facing. I call that unfair taxation. That is right, unfair taxation. You heard me.
Tbday the average, middle-class Canadian family is being taxed out of existence. When more than 50 cents out of every dollar is grabbed by the government what incentive is there to build for the future? What incentive is there to save? What incentive do we have to believe in Canada?
May 16, 1991

A fair Canada? Not with unfair taxation.
We have heard the lies and the hypocrisy about taxation in this country for years. I am not telling Canadians anything new when I recall that the former finance minister said: "Hey, the GST is great, it is going to be a visible tax". Ha, ha. Wrong.
A visible tax. Did you see it? I didn't see it. Most places say: "Our fee, our price, includes GST". That is not very visible.
Also, we heard another-I have to watch my language here because I know I must not be unparliamentary-error from Mr. Wilson, another error from the former Minister of Finance. He said: "the GST will be revenue neutral". We do not hear that any more. Revenue neutral, my eye. It is a cash cow and he knows it.

Yes, Mr. Wilson did get out of the job. I want to recall what he said, though. Mr. Wilson, the former finance minister, said that we, the middle-class taxpayers, would probably have to pay about $300 more because of the GST. He said: "If you want to help this deficit, bring it down, that is what is necessary".
Well, I'll be darned. The latest figures show that it is closer to $600. That is double.

Double what they promised us. I mean, how wrong can you be?
The government says it has been cutting costs to bring down taxes but we still have close to 40 ministries, about double what we had two decades ago. Government workers had their wages cut, but senior government officials, the so-called mandarins-I never used the word mandarin before I came to Ottawa- and the workers for the Bank of Canada, had a real sweetheart deal. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to address my fellow citizens today in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. Last Monday, the Governor General gave Canadians a clear message, one based on national unity, on the prosperity of the Canadian economy and on governmental efficiency.
Canada cannot continue to grow, prosper and develop without these three elements as part of a coherent whole. Mr. Speaker, Canada's unity involves the very existence of this great country, which was bequeathed to us by our fathers and mothers and is now lent to us by our children.

Canada cannot exist without retaining the integrity of its territory. This land has to stretch from the waters of the Atlantic Ocean to the waters of the Pacific Ocean and to the waters and icefields of the Arctic.
Canada has to include the rocky shores of Newfoundland, the rugged but grandiose expanses of Labrador, the beauty of the maritimes, the uniqueness of Quebec, the industrial structure of Ontario, the Great Lakes, the vast prairies, the mountains and beautiful coast of British Columbia. This country has to include the Yukon and its natural resources, the Northwest Territories and the Arctic. Without any one of these geographical areas, Canada is not a country.
Canada is also a country of diversified people. [Translation]
The first native inhabitants, the first immigrants from continental Europe and the British Isles and all those who followed them have worked together to populate Canada. Take one of these people away and Canada is no longer a country.
Mr. Speaker, today we must look at the situation head on. Can we afford to take actions with unimaginable consequences? No, Mr. Speaker. We all have the responsibility to weigh carefully the significance and impact of the action we take. Breaking up the country and ending arrangements that have served the interests of Canadians and Quebecers well is too risky. Is it not wiser to continue our efforts to strengthen the country! Is it
May 16, 1991

not more logical to take new approaches that will lead to constitutional arrangements that are acceptable and profitable for all citizens of Canada? The answer to this question is yes.
Let us look together for arrangements that will let Canada continue on the road to greater prosperity. Our government's initiatives are a step in the right direction. The Citizens' Forum under Keith Spicer has done good work and continues to do so. This unique unprecedented initiative has enabled very many citizens to talk about their vision of Canada.

The success of this series of initiatives by our government will lead Canadians and Quebecers to realize the importance of keeping the country together. The prosperity of the Canadian economy will also help ensure Canada's unity.
The Speech from the Throne presents Canadians with a progressive vision for the direction of the country's economy. Prosperity depends on competitiveness, the dynamism of Canadian businesses and the skill of Canadian workers. Since 1984, our government has implemented a whole series of measures to make Canadian businesses more competitive.
Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of this House and Canadians, let me mention some of them: The thorough full overhaul of the tax system; the free trade treaty with
The Address
the United States; the revision of the Financial Institutions Act; the privatization of many Crown corporations including Air Canada and Petro-Canada; the sale to the private sector of government-controlled businesses; and the implementation of regional development programs in many parts of the country. [English)
The Speech from the Throne proposes new and bold initiatives aimed at reinforcing our economic structure. I would like to quote the following from the Speech from the Throne:
-my government will work with provincial governments to ensure that Canada becomes a single, integrated market from coast to coast to coast.
This proposed initiative will cause major changes in the Canadian way of doing business internally. It will mean the elimination of policies preventing provincial agencies from buying at lower cost in other provinces. It will mean the elimination of regulations that force Canadian suppliers to sell their products abroad instead of selling them in neighbouring provinces.

Mr. Speaker, this initiative will also eliminate employment practices that hurt Canadian workers.
That is an important courageous initiative that will also contribute to the country's prosperity.
Manpower training will also receive special attention. Our workers must adjust to technological change, new work methods and new concepts of management and production.
Bill C-21 now makes available funds so that we can considerably increase our efforts to improve the skill of our labour force.
Our small and medium sized businesses in Quebec face huge manpower problems. It is most urgent that our government and the Government of Quebec conclude agreements on labour force training.
This is not the time for discord and jurisdictional quarrels. Employers and workers need immediate strong actions and the federal government has an extremely important role to play in this field, even if the hon. member for Shefford does not agree, although when he

May 16, 1991
The Address
was on the government side, he could have influenced these decisions, but I must say that he did not do so.
The Speech from the Throne also announces our government's firm intention to increase its efforts in education. Together with all my colleagues from Quebec, I applaud this initiative. We members of Parliament from Quebec in Ottawa call on our provincial colleagues to react positively to this intention.
Together, let us tell the ministers responsible, both in Quebec and in Ottawa, to leave rhetoric aside and to think of the young people who drop out of high school. That is the problem, which must be attacked resolutely.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne reveals some horrifying figures: Three high school students in ten drop out before graduation-and in some regions of the country, it is four out of ten,-and four adults in ten neither read nor do arithmetic to function properly. These data justify immediate action that must not cease until the goals set are reached.
These goals are clearly set out in the Speech from the Throne: Cutting illiteracy rates in half; ensuring that ninety percent of Canadians attain high school diplomas; doubling the number of post-secondary graduates in mathematics, science and engineering; quadrupling the training provided by employers to their employees.
Let us join forces at every level of government to achieve these goals. The prosperity of our country depends on it. The need to improve the efficiency of the machinery of government is stated in the Speech from the Throne. That part of the Speech contains a list of proposed changes.
Now, it is up to the Parliamentarians, elected representatives and government officials to set up the appropriate mechanisms.
Mr. Speaker, I want to say again that the people from remote areas, who live far away from the governmental major decision-making centres are frustrated by what they perceive to be indifference on the part of civil servants in dealing with their problems. I must admit that, while this frustration is sometimes legitimate, most civil servants try to provide the best service possible to their clients.
The problem, in my opinion, is that the decision-making process is too concentrated at the upper echelons located far from the major centres.
Regional services do exist but, more often than not, decisions are made at the head office.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the efficiency of the machinery of government calls for a genuine decentralization of the administrative decision-making process. Departments must grant a greater autonomy to their regional managers.
Those are some of my comments on the Speech from the Throne opening the third session of the Thirty-Fourth Parliament of Canada.
If we work together toward achieving the goals set by the government, we will be gratified, by the end of this mandate, to see we have helped maintain and strenghten the integrity, unity and prosperity of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this very important occasion in the life of this Parliament, which is to debate the new blueprint put forward by the government.
This is one of the signal hallmark events in the life of any parliamentary session. It should establish for all Canadians the opportunity to know where we are going, to begin to put together the kind of plan and formulation of goals that are going to be essential to deal with the kind of world we live in.
As I read and listened to the throne speech and to the debate, I wondered if we were really engaged in a serious exercise. I thought really the whole object of the government was to build up a tourist industry in Canada by convincing Canadians they do not have to go to Florida to go to Disneyland or Fantasyland. They only have to come to Ottawa and look at the performance of this government. They do not have to go down to Orlando,
Florida to see Dumbo and Goofy, they can look at the front benches of the government in the last few days to understand what kind of fantasy world is being built here in Ottawa.
The government talks about a prosperous Canada, and it talks about it sort of based on the free trade agreement and all the new economic initiatives. The reality of Canada is 100 metres in front of this building where truckers are protesting, as they are across Canada, because they are losing their jobs and they are fighting for their economic survival. TTie government says: "We will study the problem."
What can be more of a fairy tale than that enormous gap between the reality that every one sees as we walk in this building in the last days, and when we listen to members on the opposite side or the ministers who say: "We are going to build a prosperous Canada."
The government talks about caring for our children. Our children are our most important asset. The reality is, as I see in my riding, that 40 or 50 per cent of the food banks are occupied by children and their families because they cannot get enough to eat at home. Their welfare payments or their income is not enough to buy them the basic staples of our society.
Is there anything in the throne speech-although I hear a comment from the minister that yes, we are. We are going to have another study. We are going to have another committee. The government is turning Canada into one big university symposium. The only people who are going to get jobs out of this are the researchers and the appointees to new royal commissions, new committees and new study teams.
What goes on in the reality of Canada as it now exists is that we have the shame and tragedy of close to half a million children starving in this country. I have not heard any real commitment to action based upon that harsh, difficult and incredibly insensitive reality.
As a critic for external affairs, I looked again at the throne speech and have listened with some anticipation to what the government said about the world we live in. It says Canada will once again defend its interests in this world of a global economy. The harsh reality, again, is seen on the hills of Ttirkey and Iran where there are still over one million Kurdish refugees. It is seen in the depleted, tragic wastelands of Bangladesh, Sudan, Soma-
May 16, 1991

lia and Ethiopia. That is the harsh reality of the world we live in.
What does our government have to say about it? What initiatives are we going to take? What roles are we going to perform? If you listen to the throne speech, we are going to do what we have been doing up to now, which is nothing.
We fought a war just a few months ago in the gulf where we were prepared to spend close to $1 billion. We said it was a great fight for democracy and for the rule of law. It was a great opportunity to show that there will be now a new sense of international responsibility and collective security. A billion dollars to fight a war.
We had war cabinets meeting every day, and the cameras were whirling. We had the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs coming out and declaring the important initiatives. Canada was going to fight for a reduction in the arms trade. Canada was going to propose economic development. Canada was going to take the leadership in reforming the United Nations.
Is there anything in the throne speech about that? Did you read anything about what we are doing now? The arms trade is going on in the Middle East. They have just negotiated a sale of $25 billion. I did not hear anybody from the Canadian government objecting to that initiative. I did not hear anybody in the Canadian government in this new world order saying to our allies in Europe, the United States or others: "Hey, stop selling arms". That is what the Prime Minister said we were going to do during the war. But somehow we have forgotten about that obligation.
I see the tragedy taking place in the aftermath of the war; the consequences of the war, the total destruction in the countries, the refugees hanging out in the hills. Where is the incredible mobilization of Canada that we saw during the war? Where is the peace cabinet that should be mobilized to bring the resources of this country together to help these people? Is that not equally important?
I do not see any commitment in the throne speech. I do not see any initiative by the Canadian government. I
The Address
do not see any action being promised. It is a total absence and omission.
Instead, it fired some 300 people from the Department of External Affairs, people who were working on proposals to deal with the spread of arms; people who were working on UN reform. These people who were working on these very initiatives no longer have jobs.
Of course, the new minister of external affairs has set an incredibly new launch in her tenure as a minister by totally denying her responsibility for the action of the department and is trying to lay the blame on civil servants. What kind of performance is this government going to expect from its prime public servants when it has trespassed upon the fundamental, essential, value of ministerial accountability. It is a great way to start the new world order from a Canadian point of view by telling your department it can hang out to dry. That is an awfully good way for this government to start leading its new interventions in the world with a minister, who in a cowardly way, refuses to take responsibility for what that department does. That is a great way to get started.
Once again we are back in the world of fantasy land. We are back living in a world that really does not exist. The government side is weaving and spinning in a world of make believe, of magic. Unfortunately, the only people who believe it are the members of the government, because nobody else out there does. Nobody else believes there is a real commitment to action. No one else believes there really is a plan in mind.
The harsh reality is that when it comes to dealing with the problems of Canada and the problems of the world, this government is bankrupt of ideas. It has nothing to offer except more study, more examination, more review, more inquiries, nothing that would give any sense that it knows where it is going. There is no blueprint here. All we have is a prescription for navel gazing, hoping somehow that there will be some magical turn of events because it does not know how to control matters any longer.
What is sad about it is that it has not learned from its mistakes. It has not learned that there are serious fundamental problems in this whole trade arrangement with the United States that is leading to enormous losses of jobs in steel, automobiles, food processing and agricul-

May 16, 1991
The Address
ture. Jobs are being lost every day because we did not negotiate the right deal.
However, the government does not say: "Well, okay, we have had a couple of years to see how it is going. Here is how we can change it. Here is how we can renegotiate it. Here is how we can improve upon it. Here is what we should do about it". It says; "Hey, it is wonderful".
Tell the unemployed workers in the steel mills or the food processing plants how wonderful it is and they will tell you that once again you are living a great lie.
The harsh reality again is that there is no sense of realism about what it is doing. Instead it promises that it is now going to renegotiate a deal with Mexico, for North American free trade, but without knowing why, without knowing where it wants to go, without knowing what kind of conditions.
President Bush at least had the good sense to set certain objectives, dealing with social, environmental and labour problems. We have not had a word, a whisper. There is nothing in the throne speech to show that we have learned any lessons about how to deal with the difficult world of international trade.
Again, dealing with the incredibly important problem of national unity, we have a promise for another committee to study the works of other committees, who were studying the works of other committees. We are sort of beginning to chase our tail on this issue. The Prime Minister says one thing and then another. We may have a referendum, we may not have a referendum, we may have this, we may have that. We have no sense of where we are going.
As a westerner I am surprised and extremely disappointed, that when discussing changing how Ottawa works, the whole fundamental question of Senate reform was totally ignored.
I would like to read into the record a statement by Gordon Robertson, one of the most senior and respected public servants in this country for many long years. I quote from his book A House Divided where he wrote: "Agreement on the Senate was the key to Confederation in 1867. Agreement on its reform could be the key to the impasse that today threatens the renewal of our federalism for the future."
One of the most important and admired public servants who has studied the Constitution says the key to
the impasse of trying to find reconciliation between east and west, of giving the regions the feeling that they belong in a full sense, is Senate reform.
I looked closely at the throne speech, I used a microscope, I changed my glasses, I examined it, perused it. There is not one word about our willingness, our preparation to change the Senate. It is totally ignored. Yet I know that last month during the parliamentary break when I travelled throughout western Canada as chairman of a committee of our own caucus on constitutional matters it came up in every single meeting. It has the same symbolic importance in western Canada as the issue of a distinct or unique society has in Quebec. The same feeling of providing a recognition of belonging.
Yet, a throne speech which tries to set out the new blueprint for federalism completely misses the point.
There has to be Senate reform. It is a way of righting the imbalances, inequities and inequalities that have existed in federalism since its inception. There is not one federal state in the world that does not have a second chamber which works effectively to represent regional interests.
Through quirks of history ours does not. It is not an elected body, it does not have the credibility or the legitimacy of being democratically elected by the people. Therefore, its ability to provide a check and balance upon the role of the executive, which is dictated to by the majority of members from the heavily populated provinces, is constantly undermined. We see it repeated time and time again in many decisions, I don't have to place in the record of the House that history. It is seen and felt in a palpable way.
There are all kinds of proposals around. Mr. Robertson, in his book, discusses all of them and comes up with what I think is a pretty fair proposal, an elected Senate that has effective powers to provide checks and balances, that can say yes or no to appointments to Crown agencies, to Crown boards, to various appointments. It could provide protection for language and culture at the national level, rather than relying simply on provincial powers.
There could be an election based upon proportional representation to ensure that minorities are reflected in that body. The elections could be staggered every two years in a six-year term to create a kind of mini-election
May 16, 1991

to test the government so it would have to be conscious of changes in the mood of the public and their concerns.
There are some good ideas around, ideas that we have promoted. The 1986 resolution, passed at our own policy convention, set out a very clear statement of our commitment to that reform. There is nothing from the government on that crucial issue.
I say to the new Minister of Constitutional Affairs, who is from western Canada, that no one should know better than he how important it is that Senate reform become part of the package. I am not saying this in a partisan sense. I am simply saying there will be no agreement on any new constitutional package until we have a commitment and agreement that we will pursue Senate reform based upon a democratic election, upon effective powers, and making it more equal.
That has to be the hallmark of any new proposal. It is something that is important because in western Canada we recognize the importance of reorganizing and restructuring our own arrangements.
A week or so ago I put out a proposal saying that the prairie provinces have to come together in some form of union. They have to begin merging and integrating many of the economic activities of the prairie region, such as telecommunications, training, and transportation. We are small and do not have the same kind of critical mass, resources, and people and as a result we have to begin combining our resources and combining our energies to make it work. There are similar proposals in the Atlantic provinces for the same thing.
We are prepared to restructure this country. It is important. We recognize the crucial challenges in the global economy. It is not going to happen until there is a willingness at the federal level to make changes. That means not just dealing with Senate reform but reforming many of the regulatory bodies of the federal government to make them work at a regional level, and ensuring that transportation is tailored and blueprinted to the concerns of that region.
It means using some of the regional development funds, instead of using them as slush funds for individual businesses, to start rebuilding the infrastructure, the
The Address
training facilities, and the schools of those regions so they can get up to par, so they can begin to improve those areas.
There is an awful lot more reform and remodelling that has to be done than simply having another committee go to work on it. On the crucial question of constitutional amendment, we could use the Victoria formula. A prairie union could provide its own veto for that part of the world and ensure that westerners do not feel they are being left out, like they are second class citizens in their own country.
Those are the kinds of proposals I would have expected in a throne speech that said we are at a crossroads, a turning point. I would have expected a clear, unmistakable agenda of action, proposing how to deal with problems of the world, how to deal with our own economic problems, and how to deal with regional problems.
That was not in it. Instead, we have a brochure from Disneyland outlining how to pretend what is going on as opposed to getting down to work, getting down to action.
I know my time is about through-I would love to be able to spend more hours with you, and I know that you would love that as well. The message we are really trying to give is that we all recognize the importance of breaking out of conventional ways of putting our heads to work, of coming up with ideas that Canadians can really understand and that indicate the political system is working well. Credibility and belief in the political system will not be achieved by tinkering with a little bit of machinery. It is going to come about by clearly demonstrating that the people they elect know where they are going, can provide some leadership, have a sense of purpose, and know what the blueprint should be. If that is the criteria for leadership then the throne speech is an abysmal failure.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to ask a question that comes from the Canada West Foundation. The member in his speech talked about the free trade agreement. The foundation said that Canada's merchandise trade with the U.S. jumped to $17.4 billion last year, up from $14.2 billion in 1988. More impressively, direct investment in Canada exceeded Canadian direct investment in other countries by $4.3 billion in 1990, the first time in a decade that there has been a net inflow of funds. In 1988, just before free trade, there was an outflow of $2.5 billion.
Looking at only the flow of direct investment between Canada and the United States, there was a similar reversal. In 1990 Canada attracted $800 million more in direct U.S. investment than the U.S. did in Canada, and in 1988 the U.S. had attracted $3.8 billion more. This suggests that overseas investors see Canada as an increasingly attractive place.
This information comes from the Canada West Foundation. I remind the member for Winnipeg South Centre that this was put together by a business consultant based in Winnipeg who concluded in his report: "Despite the bad economic news of 1990, including confirmation of a recession, export sales to the U.S. have been a shining star. The bottom line is that Canadian trade with the U.S. has been basically business as usual".
This comes from western Canada, part of the country that he represents. It seems to differ with the partisan comments that he has suggested. I would like him to comment on these particular numbers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not conscious that my remarks were particularly partisan, but I am very pleased to respond to the question. It was totally non-partisan and objective as we well know, as has been my tradition in this House over the past 12 or 13 years.
The member points out figures provided by the Canada West Foundation. I think he might more accurately look at some of the figures provided by agents of Statistics Canada. They point out that we have the highest current account deficit in the history of this country, close to $20 billion. The net outflow of funds on dividends, profits, and intercorporate transfers is at its highest level ever. What is really happening in this country is that we are haemorrhaging in terms of flow of dollars outward.
Also, let us take a look at direct investment figures. If we break them down in their particulars, we find that a large proportion of direct investment is going into takeovers and acquisitions. I think the last figure provided by Statistics Canada was close to 95 per cent. It is not going into new investments or new businesses. It is going into taking over Canadian companies which are not able to survive.
It is also important to point out in terms of those figures that one of the reasons there is an inflow is that we have a God-awful, unacceptable, high rate of interest and high dollar. They have to be kept propped up in order to bring in money to replace that which is flowing out. In order to replace what is being haemorrhaged, we
May 16, 1991

have to provide an unnatural pool of money for blood transfusions. That is the real problem.
It is only, as our leader said in his opening speech, when we have a more realistic economic policy that we can begin to get our economic house in order. Then we will not have to rely upon all that direct investment, simply short-term Treasury bill investments, to prop up the economy. We know we are in a vicious circle caused by much of the openings that took place under that trade agreement.
Third, I ask the hon. gentleman-and I know he is a serious member of Parliament-to step across the lawn and talk to the truckers today and see how they feel about the economic policies of this government. He should go down to the food processing plants that have been closed in Portage la Prairie, the steel plants in southwestern Ontario or auto parts plants.
There is one basic fallacy in the comments the member made, and I am sure he made it mistakenly. He said: "We may be selling a little bit more high-tech but, after all, things like agriculture, fish, auto parts-all these other things-are not doing so well any more". I will tell you why they are not doing so well. It is because of that trade agreement. We lost control of our resources, and those other industries that he mentioned happened to be the backbone of the industry of Canada.
