speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by expressing my congratulations to the member for Saint-Maurice and the member for Regina-Wascana for the excellent way in which they began this debate.
This session of Parliament will be more important than most, perhaps more important than any before it. During this time, our country will either agree to go ahead or decide to close down. That determines our obligations today. As all the leaders in this House have said, this is
not about the preferences of a party or the agenda of a government. The only agenda is Canada. That has never been a partisan purpose before and it will not be now.
Those of us sitting here are far from perfect, as individuals or as a Parliament. Whatever our past failings, we are determined that we shall not fail Canada. I understand fully that the non-partisan approach requires the government to involve all of Parliament in basic decisions. That is why the Prime Minister stated explicitly yesterday our willingness to accept sensible proposals from any party or parliamentarian. That is why I began my new responsibilities by reaching out deliberately to Canadians who had felt excluded in the past- native leaders, northerners, western Canadians. We have an obligation to listen, to learn and to lead, and I know we must do all three if we are to succeed.
No individual, party or government is going to compel Canada to continue. Canadians must decide whether we wish to keep our country. That is a decision for all of us.
Elected members of this House have an extra obligation. We have to ensure that the issues are clear, that the stakes are understood, and that Canadians have the chance to consider every reasonable proposal to renew and to save this country. We will need a lot of help in that work. We cannot lock ourselves into old ways which Canadians no longer respect or trust.
Neither should we lightly put aside our parliamentary process which has earned its legitimacy through 124 years of Canadian experience. Parliament needs to be reformed, not abandoned, and on behalf of the government I am prepared to consider any serious proposal any member might make as to how we involve Canadians who are not elected.
Involving them does not mean that we should step aside from our most basic responsibilities. None of us would deny that this country is in crisis. This crisis can also be an opportunity, a new beginning, a journey of liberation from the worst of our past and a freedom to build upon the best within all of us. I believe that Canadians across this country are beginning to see it that way too.
They are beyond simple despair at how things have gone wrong, and are wondering how to help set things right. This is a time for this country to reflect on our past and get to know it, to reflect on our present and decide
May 16, 1991

how to improve it, and to look ahead to our future to determine how best to achieve it together.

Mr. Speaker, our plan consists of four separate phases. Phase one is nearing its conclusion. By July 1, we will have received the reports of the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future and the Special Joint Committee on the Process for Amending the Constitution of Canada. Both have done a good job, and the government will examine their conclusions with all the attention and care the views of Canadians deserve.
The next step will be the tabling of a set of proposals on how to reform the country. These proposals will be detailed, they will be specific and they will be published. They will not remain in the private domain, known only to a chosen few. All Canadians will know our vision of the future.
These proposals will not be final. However, during the third phase, Canadians will have a chance to tell us what they think. A joint committee of Parliament will meet Canadians across the country to hear their views. The committee will hold public hearings, not to discuss the country's future in genenral but to discuss specific changes.
The committee's mission and purpose will be clearcut. It will be asked to consider concrete proposals for constitutional change. It will seek comments from Canadians and make recommendations to the government. The committee will have discussions with committees or similar groups of members of the various provincial and territorial legislatures, on how they will proceed and the witnesses they wish to invite. This will be more than just a matter of joint hearings. It will be a full-fledged association. The resulting dialogue can then be used to build a national consensus.

A major priority will be an intensive dialogue with the aboriginal community whose constitutional concerns must be addressed in this committee while simultaneously its economic and social concerns are the subject of a royal commission inquiry.
The Address
In the final step, we expect Parliament will propose reforms that will set this country on a sound and sure course for the next century. In order to leave open as many options as possible, this House will be asked to pass legislation which would enable the people of Canada to express themselves directly in a referendum.
It is not our preference nor is it our intention to seek to resolve complex, constitutional questions by way of referendum but we believe it is prudent for the federal government to have the full authority to conduct a Canadian referendum-

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
-should that become the best way to achieve consensus on defining our future together.
We are prepared to consider other methods of consulting Canadians, including any proposals that might come from the mixed committee, the Beaudoin-Edwards committee.
I do not believe there has ever been a more open process put in place for the people of Canada to decide themselves the destiny of our country. I wish to turn to some of the tasks which I believe are in front of us in the months ahead.
First, this time constitutional change must address several issues simultaneously. This cannot be a Quebec round, an aboriginal round or a Senate round. We have to make progress on many fronts together. This must be a Canada round.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Second, we must be guided by a sense of both pragmatism and history. We want a country that works well and works together in one of the most challenging periods in world history.
The only way for our reforms to succeed is to respect the special nature of this country, including the objective reality that Quebec is a distinct society.
Third, the country must get to know itself better. The stories which suffuse our history are extraordinary. They are stories of achievement, of strength in the face of adversity, of a unity built on diversity. We do not tell those stories so we do not know them. Let us tell them again. Nostalgia will not hold this country together, but knowledge can.

May 16, 1991
The Address
We need to know our history, but we also need to get to know each other better. In Yellowknife last week, Mayor Pat McMahon brought a few people together to talk to me about Canada. One woman observed of Canada, and I quote her: "Everybody feels misunderstood". That says two things. First, misunderstanding is widespread but, second, for most of us the priority is to have others understand us. It is not a one way street.
If we want to keep and build this country, citizens everywhere must work at understanding why other Canadians have priorities different from their own. Quebecers must try to understand why western Canadians feel that institutions like the Senate must be changed fundamentally. Western Canadians must try to understand why recognition of a distinct society is so important to Quebec.
Those of us whose ancestors came to Canada from somewhere else must try to understand that aboriginal claims are about respect as much as they are about money.
Fourth, there is a real desire in this country for information. Canadians want to base their decisions on evidence and not on ideology. They are ready to move beyond accusation to deliberation. They want to know what unity gives them. They want to know what taking away unity would leave.
Sometimes I think we talk too much about our differences and too little about our common Canadian citizenship. I celebrate the diversity of this country, but the real strength of Canada is that we have made these different parts work together. That has required a basic respect for others that is not at all common in the world. We Canadians use our gifts of wealth and freedom to advance our neighbours' interests, not just our own. That sense of duty to a larger community is evident everywhere in Canada. We have to make more of that common Canadian citizenship.

According to any standard, we, as Canadians, have accomplished a great deal. We are free, we are prosperous, we are tolerant and we are educated. Taken individually, these qualities are exceptional. Together, they
have made Canada a country that is both unafraid to tread uncharted paths and that cares for its people.
Mr. Speaker, it cannot be repeated often enough that the integrity of Canadian values is part and parcel to the integrity of this country. Canadians did not choose the path of mutual respect because they felt like it but because our diversity implies the mutual respect of our component parts, so that our relations can be peaceful and productive.
Canadians did not choose the path of tolerance because it was fashionable but because different cultures must work together if they are to survive.
Mr. Speaker, most Canadians have other, more pressing concerns and priorities than changing the Constitution. They have to look after the education of then-children, maintain their prosperity and keep their neighbourhoods safe and clean. However, they must also keep pace with the rest of the world.

People can unplug their phones, countries cannot. While we are deciding whether Canada should continue, other countries are moving forward without us. What price are we paying for quarrelling at home while others are focusing on the future? What price are we paying while others are preoccupied with innovating, educating, changing and competing? Unlike Peter Sellers' last movie, countries do not succeed by just being there.
I am not saying that Canada should stay together just because some accountant or economist might say it makes sense. Canada is not a corporate merger but being poor is no foundation for doing anything. I do not know of one economic argument which says that being smaller means being better.
If there were such an argument, Europe would not be uniting. If there were such an argument, Asia would not be trading. If there were such an argument, Confederation would never have happened. Our ancestors would have seen a better life apart than they found together.
If that was the decision in the middle of the 19th century, when the global economy had barely begun, how on earth can it be different now when the global village is at our doorstep, and at our doorstep forever.
May 16, 1991

Whatever the options in the past, whatever the differences Canadians have had, our advantage in the future is to be together as one strong, large, effective country.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I believe we have time. In 1864, Confederation was constructed in four short months between the conference in Quebec City and the conference in Charlottetown. Although our problems may be more complex, surely we can begin to save a country in the time it took to build one.
In 1865, George Brown, one of the Fathers of Confederation made a statement. He had not been a fan of Confederation, but he came to be a convert. He said, and I quote:
We are endeavouring to adjust harmoniously greater difficulties than have plunged other countries into all the horrors of civil war. We are striving to settle forever issues hardly less momentous than those that have rent the United States of America, and are now exposing it to all the horrors of civil war. Have we not then great cause of thankfulness that we have found a better way for the solution of our troubles than that which has entailed in other countries, such deplorable results.
Canada is still the better way. The world knows it. Our ancestors knew it when they chose to come here from around the globe. Canadians know it today. It is our obligation to build that better way, not to discard it, knowing the value of our achievement and knowing that we can make it better still.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister had a very effective speech. As he put the four stages of the process before us, it certainly cleared up some of the concerns I have and I am sure other people have.
Having been on the Beaudoin-Edwards committee and knowing that everybody who came before us said that public participation was critical to the process, I had hoped the minister would come up with proposals that the public would have had a chance to discuss. I will ask about that again in my second question. But from that discussion, a new set of proposals, some reinforced or some discarded, and then more public participation after it had been looked at again.
I am wondering if there is to be a two-stage public participation in the process.
Second, I cannot believe that we have to wait until September to get the proposals. I think everybody in Canada knows that the Senate and Parliament have to be reformed. The Supreme Court could easily be, by bring-
The Address
ing together the provinces to look at it. The distribution of powers does not need unanimity. There was not one expert who said it was the Constitution that was to blame. They said it was the process that was used around Meech. There was not one expert who did not point out that we had two amendments since the new Constitution was in place that passed, and only one failed.
I just cannot believe, with the government having a majority here and in the Senate, that we cannot get together and reform the institutions within our own jurisdiction this summer. I do not know any Canadians, since I crossed Canada, who felt that we were giving them leadership, from this place down to the people, in the areas that we have control over.
The other thing is the power of spending. That is something that the government can talk about and talk about immediately. I do not believe that you can roll the dice, come February, to the Allaire or the Belanger-Campeau committees and not have time next fall to undo it. I know the feelings out there and I am sure the minister is well aware of the feelings right across Canada. There is a hope that we can come together in Canada and redefine ourselves but I do think there is a lot that could be done immediately to make that process a lot easier.
I am wondering if the minister would tell me why the proposals cannot be done, and some of the things done immediately.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is no question about two realities concerning public opinion: One is that there is a profound cynicism about existing institutions, and each of us will attribute that to different origins, but there is no question about the reality of it. There is also no question about the fact that that, if we simply succumb to it, it is corrosive, that could be destructive of this country. What we have to do is not succumb to criticisms of our institutions but to prove that by reforming them we can make them work better. That cynicism is there and we have to take account of it.
The second reality, flowing from the first, is that Canadians very much want to take part. Individual Canadians do, but so do some particular Canadian groups. The hon. member has been engaged in this process more intensively over the last few months than I have been but since my appointment to this portfolio I have, for example, made a point of meeting with native leaders, going to the north and speaking to people who see their interests not simply in terms of their own

May 16, 1991
The Address
particular interest, but also in terms of the regions they represent or the groups from which they come.
Speaking of public participation, we have two processes that end the July 1. The hon. member is part of the joint committee and we have the Spicer committee. There was a lot of scepticism about the Spicer committee but I think that process has engendered a great deal of participation and a lot of originality across the country.
Public consultation cannot stop. We all have obligations to carry it forward, and I have to find ways in which some of the work that was started by Spicer can be carried on. It is important that the next phase of public consultation not be about issues in general, but about specific proposals that can put things in a general context of reform. We are not talking here simply about changing institutions within the federal jurisdiction; we are talking about basic changes in Canada, including changes in the way we see ourselves and changes in attitude. There needs to be some over-all context within which we act and we are trying, hoping and expecting to have it ready for the fall. We expect to be able to put before this House in the fall an over-all position as to how these changes which we must pursue together can be put together to advance the country.
Then the discussion, the next phase of public participation, will be a phase which will allow individual Canadians to focus specifically upon particular proposals placed in a Canadian context that have been put forward by the government.
We will welcome amendments, changes and improvements in that process. We think that is the best way to take account of what is being done now and to ensure that Canadians have a constructive opportunity to help define the future of the country.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands. I would like to recognize the hon. member for Parkdale and also the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Shef-ford, but I only have six minutes.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin my remarks by congratulating the minister on his appointment to this portfolio and to wish
him well. I hope that the esteem in which he is held in this country will bring a resolution.
Having said that, he knows what is coming next. The remarks in his speech were well-suited. He talked about reaching out to those who felt excluded, and as a member of the Beaudoin-Edwards committee, that was the over-riding theme. I caution and urge him and all of us to have the political courage as politicians to step back from this issue, look at it and take the condemnation of the Canadian people sincerely.
We deserve it. This is a wonderful country we have, and we are at the risk of losing it. As you, Sir, know better than most-people, we have a wonderful country. People outside of this country are wondering what we are on about here when they are talking about issues of survival and here we are navel gazing.
That criticism is real. It is very sincere. Please do not dismiss a constituent assembly made up of politicians and those who have felt excluded. Please do not exclude that option, because that is something that I think is a balance. Please do not exclude that.
My second point is with respect to your reference to a Canadian referendum. Referenda have been divisive tools in Canada's history. My question is: What do you think would constitute a majority? Would Quebec need to have its referendum on the same issue? The west? The north? The aboriginal people? This is the complexity.
As one of the witnesses at the Beaudoin-Edwards committee hearings pointed out to the committee, any parliamentary reform is like a Rubik's cube. You change one thing and the whole thing changes. We in this place have to have the wisdom to be able to see what those changes will bring.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, on a referendum.
I have said publicly that in our view a referendum cannot be used to force any group of Canadians to do something that it does not want to do. We are in a situation in which the Government of Canada does not have the legal authority that we require for the kind of
May 16, 1991

consultation that might become necessary as we seek to achieve the broadest possible consensus in the country. We are not introducing it because we intend to use it; we are introducing it because we think we may have need for it and we think it would be prudent to have that in place.
With respect to the other question, I agree with the hon. member's comment about the force of Canadian opinion. I do not intend to reject in advance anything that might be proposed by the Beaudoin-Edwards committee.
Here is the challenge that I think we all have to look at in the next little while. We have a parliamentary system. It is heavily criticized, but it has served the country well for over a century. Churchill once called it the worst system of government in the world except for all the others, and that reality continues.
We have that base. How do we add to that base in this committee process to make all Canadians, particularly people who have felt excluded, feel more a part of the process? I have some ideas. Some of the proposals put in the throne speech are regarding working with legislators from the territories and from the provinces. That has never been done before. That is an innovation that may be helpful. There are others we are prepared to consider, and I say very sincerely that I would very much welcome practical proposals from any member of the House as to means in which we can combine the fundamental nature of a parliamentary committee with the necessity to involve people who felt excluded before.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to compliment the minister on his appointment and his new role and wish him well and success. He will be missed in the external affairs portfolio where we had a very close working relationship.
He is looking for proposals and I would like to toss this proposal to his committee. I was bom and raised in Saskatchewan. I went to a one-room rural school. In Grade 1, the teacher made up her own rules. She had the entire school stand up-the entire school being 30 students-and salute the Canadian flag, which was a little different than the one beside you now.
We all had to salute the flag and we had to recite "I pledge allegiance to this flag and to the country for
The Address
which it stands." I realized later that she had adopted a modified version of the American pledge to the flag.
In all the committee hearings that have been going on across the country, the one thing we are not hearing is: What does it mean to be a Canadian citizen?
As a Canadian citizen what are my obligations, what are my duties, to this country? Every group says: "What is in this for me? When you modify the Constitution, what would it give me". It is high time we turned this around and asked: "What can I do for my country?"
I would like to see that in the preamble to the Canadian Constitution where we talk about goals in education. Every student going through the school system, regardless of province or territory, should memorize such a pledge. I think the next generations would be proud to keep their various cultural backgrounds, but the one thing every Canadian would have in common is growing up saying: "I pledge allegiance to this flag and to the country for which it stands".

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Grade 1 classes in Saskatchewan were larger than they were in Alberta.
We do not want to instruct people to salute our flag but create conditions where Canadians everywhere choose to celebrate our flag. We will need a great deal of help in this. I take it as part of the responsibilities that are now mine to try to evoke in Canada a much stronger and truer sense of Canadian citizenship, of common Canadian citizenship.
I agree with the member that it is essential, but it is something that we have to draw from the people rather than try to impose upon them. In this unusual time of real anguish in the country, when Canadians are genuinely concerned about the future of the country, we have a better prospect of doing that than we ever had before. We have to know more about our country. I am appalled at how little Canadians know about the history of this extraordinary country. I am appalled that anyone could think that a country like this is dull. The other day I was in Iqaluit. In the bright light of night Canadians were going out to the edge of the ice floes to hunt seals. At the same time in southern Canada, some of the best scientists any country anywhere in the world could develop were working on ways to move into the future of high technology.

May 16, 1991
The Address
We are a country that has everything. We do not know ourselves well enough and that is part of the reason we are in the difficulty we face now. I look forward to help from the House and from other Canadians to try to create a much more striking sense of a common Canadian citizenship.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know there is not much time and I want to respond to some of the comments made by the minister.
I quoted in my own speech the comment made by Gordon Robertson who, he knows, is a highly respected commentator on constitutional affairs. He said: "Agreement on the Senate was the key to Confederation in 1867. Agreement on its reform could be the key to the impasse that today threatens renewal of our federalism for the future."
In the throne speech there was no mention of Senate reform. The minister in the past has been slightly negative about the proposal and has rejected it. I want to know if the minister is prepared to say today that he will support an initiative to reform the Senate, to make it an elected body, a more equal body, and one that has effective powers. This would allow us to have a true federalism with a second chamber that could provide the balance that our country needs.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have never rejected Senate reform. It is important in this debate that we all read one another's statements carefully. I will read his carefully.
Not only will I support Senate reform, I will be proposing Senate reform as part of the proposals we bring forward. I would add to the observation that the hon. member made. Yes, I think there should be institutional reform, probably not just the Senate, because I think Canadians from our part of the country want more than just the Senate changed. In fact, there may be institutions more important than the Senate. The Senate has a great symbolic importance but there are also other urgent issues. We cannot this time, for example, ignore the concerns of Canadian aboriginal people. Those concerns too must be given the highest possible priority and we intend to do that.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for his speech, but throughout his
statement, he somewhat trivialized the Quebec issue by saying: Listen, fundamentally, what Quebec wants is an emphasis on the distinct society, period. You know that is totally untrue and that Quebec's demands, even the traditional ones, go far beyond the concept of a distinct society.
What amazed me in the Throne Speech, since we are talking about that framework, is that how the minister, who should be sensitive to the Quebec symbol, namely in the area of education-and I don't need to remind him of the words of Maurice Duplessis and others-could allow his government to intrude in the area of education, which is the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, particularly of Quebec? The minister is aware that, for example, on the issue of vocational training, in Quebec there is not a consensus but unanimity on the full repatriation of the whole issue of vocational training.
How can the minister explain to me today that his government, which wants to hold out its hand to Quebecers once again, is raising its fist instead?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
will give two short answers, Mr. Speaker.
First, on the subject of education, it is clearly stated in the Speech from the Throne that we will fully and completely respect the provincial jurisdiction in that matter. But it is also true that the federal government already spends billions of dollars every year on education and that we are going through an education crisis in this country. This is an issue that will require greater cooperation between the various levels of government and, in fact, between all sectors of our society.
Second, in response to the allegation that I trivialized the Quebec issue, I want to tell the hon. member that I have been a member of this House for eighteen years. I came from Alberta and was unilignual. I learned French by myself and I can speak it. I am not a member of the French Academy, but I can speak the language rather efficiently. I am not the only one. There are several members-the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville is one, and so is the President, Mr. Fraser, to name a couple-who come from various parts of the country geographically remote from Quebec and who, since they were elected, have displayed a willingness to respect the uniqueness and distinctiveness of that province, not only
May 16, 1991

in words but by their actions. I have been active myself on national issues, in Quebec and elsewhere defending Quebec, throughout my career in this place.
I am not the one trivializing Quebec today, neither do I intend to trivialize its future. I want to secure a strong future for the people of Quebec and the way to achieve that is to be part of a large country, not a small one.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The time alloted to questions and comments has elapsed. On debate. The hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to intervene in this debate following the comments of the right hon. Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs.
I could not help but smile when I heard many of the remarks made by the minister. I heard him say that the federal government would put forward a proposal for constitutional change by September and that the government would not be tied to these changes, that it would welcome changes and improvements to the proposal.
I could not help but feel that we have come a long way from the seamless web, the ill-fated proposal that was debated in this House a year or two ago, which could not be changed, not one word, comma or period.
Yes, the minister has listened to his critics. Time will tell whether a leopard can truly change its spots. We will see whether this government will, indeed, speak for the national interest, not in the speeches that we are hearing today in this House but through the proposals it will table and its actions in the months ahead.

It is with interest that I listened yesterday to the Prime Minister's speech on the Constitution. I was glad to hear him finally admit that what matters is Canada and Canada above all.
After seven years, he admits that we now have to talk in favour of the national interest. He said, and I quote: "That the next round will be a Canadian round." Moreover, he talked about the need to create a national market for securities, and to exempt trust companies
The Address
from the overregulation of eleven governments. His speech, like the one made by the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs, made me smile.
The Prime Minister finally listened to his critics. It was said a few years ago that he did not respect the national interest. Today, he is telling us that the national interest must be paramount. It was said that his role had been limited to that of an arbiter. Yesterday, the Prime Minister said that he must not act as an arbiter, that he must fight for the national interest.
The question, Mr. Speaker, is to know whether we can trust this new talk by the Prime Minister. Can we really trust him to keep his word? Will he really fight for the national interest this time? Time will tell. We will see in the coming months when the government will put forward its proposals on Constitutional reform and we will see it by its deeds, not by the words pronounced in this debate on the Speech from the Throne.
The Prime Minister also talked about economy and education. He listed a few problems that you are no doubt familiar with. Thirty per cent of high school students drop out before graduation. Forty per cent of adults cannot read nor count well enough to perform day-to-day tasks. The Canadian industry devotes to the training of workers only one half of what is devoted to it by the U.S. industry, one fifth by the Japanese industry and one eighth by the German industry.
The government now wants to set up national standards with regard to education. In the coming weeks, the government will table a discussion paper as a guide for the public debate, which should lead us to some solutions.
Today, seven years after being elected, the government is proposing a debate. What has the government done for seven years? Didn't it have the responsibility to take action in those areas, to give an example, to show leadership in the areas that it would now like to draw to the attention of Canadians through a debate?
The debate proposed by the government is an admission of failure. It is the admission, that we have lost seven years during which the government should have taken action to ensure that Canadians have access to quality education and that businesses in our country do enough research and development. On the contrary,

May 16, 1991
The Address
Mr. Speaker, we saw several measures that went against those objectives.

In the throne speech the government also says that it wants to develop "a learning culture". I am apprehensive about the use of the phrase "learning culture". For some time students of Canada's science and technology policy have taken to attributing our deficiencies in science and technology to our failure to develop a science culture or a research culture.
What is meant by that is a culture which values knowledge and education and which would place top priority on developing Canada's human resources. The very use of the word "culture" is an indication of the difficulty in changing directions. A cultural change, with all it implies, is seen as the necessary condition for building public support for policy changes and for ensuring that there is a real priority for these changes in the federal and provincial halls of power.
By definition, a cultural change is something that will take a long time. The idea that we need to develop a learning culture or a science culture has become an explanation for failure. When the government uses this phrase you have to ask yourself whether the need for a cultural change is not being used as an excuse for further inaction. This is the caution which I want to draw to the attention of Canadians.
Let us take a closer look at the proposal to establish Canada-wide goals in education. The government says it would like to see "Canada-wide goals established for the year 2000". Reading this literally, this appears to mean that the government would like to see these goals established by the year 2000. It is not saying that it will reach these goals by then, but that it will establish them by then. The government appears to be suggesting, in other words, that it will take nine more years to establish goals relating to education.
Is this what the government means? Is the government suggesting that it will take nine years to establish these goals? I cannot believe this is what the government is proposing.
I would hope that this statement will be clarified and that the Prime Minister will tell us that this is not what is intended but rather that these goals will be established shortly. I recognize it may take a year or two. The
negotiations or the understanding that we have to arrive at about these goals should be part and parcel of the redefinition of the country that we are currently engaged in. Certainly these goals should be arrived at in the next year or two and we should start to take action aimed at reaching them.
Even with such a clarification, Canadians should understand that the throne speech is ambiguous. Many may think that the government is suggesting that we could reach those targets by the year 2000, that we could double the number of graduates in science and engineering and that we could reduce illiteracy substantially within a period of nine years. If that is what the government is suggesting, it is unrealistic. It is impossible to double the number of post-secondary graduates in mathematics, the sciences and engineering in such a short time, as has been amply demonstrated in study after study produced by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council.
In his speech yesterday the Prime Minister gave us a big lecture on the need for fiscal discipline. We in our party share the view of many Canadians that the federal fiscal deficit is a serious economic and political problem. Our leader notably did not make a single spending commitment in the leadership campaign. We agree that the federal fiscal deficit is a serious problem. We also agree that achieving low levels of inflation is an important objective. There is no disagreement with these objectives.
But we have to ask ourselves what is the government's record with respect to these objectives. The inflation rate today is about 7 per cent compared with 3.8 per cent inflation when the Conservatives first took office. The deficit is forecast to be $30.5 billion, which is $2 billion higher than the forecast in the budget a year ago. Contrast that with the statement of the former Minister of Finance in his first budget in 1985 that he would reduce the deficit by the end of the decade to $18 billion.
Before I go on, I just want to remind you again, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance missed the mark by the small sum of some $12.5 billion. He was predicting in his first budget that he would get the deficit down to $18 billion by the end of the decade. It is now $30.5 billion. He missed the mark by some $12.5 billion.
I find it quite outrageous to hear the Prime Minister giving us lectures about fiscal discipline and about the need to keep a budget when his government does not know the first thing about it.
May 16, 1991

It is precisely because of the government's failure to achieve the objectives it set for itself that many Canadians are having increasing doubts about the Conservatives' ability to manage the economy, to put it mildly.
While I agree that the federal fiscal deficit is a serious economic problem, it is not the source of our problems. The Canadian disease, if I may put it that way, relates to our inability to keep pace with global economic and technological change. After seven years this government must bear some responsibility for not leading the way.
I would like to read from an article published about a month and a half ago by the current chairman of the Science Council of Canada. She recited many of the sorry statistics that we have become so familiar with. She said: "We have lost a great deal of international competitive advantage we held some 30 or 40 years ago. Our standard of living has slipped accordingly and we have simply failed to anticipate environmental reality". She went on to say: "There is no use searching for a Canadian policy to cope with this crisis. We don't have a national policy".
The chairman of the Science Council of Canada is no slouch. When she says we do not have a national policy and there is no use searching for a Canadian policy, I think that Canadians by and large stand up and take notice. This is a statement that was not made eight or nine years ago. This was a statement made on March 31 of this year, seven years after this government took office, seven and eight years after the Prime Minister in the run-up to the 1984 election promised to correct the very ills which he is again talking about in this throne speech.
Canadians can no longer afford ambiguity in action and absence of national leadership. We cannot wait for changing attitudes. We cannot wait a generation. Difficult choices have to be made now. These choices say a lot about our country and its priorities.
For example, should we be investing in Hibernia or James Bay II or would we be better off investing the same kinds of resources in research and development?
The Address
Canadians again should not have to wait a generation for answers to these questions.
We have a very practical example in the last day or two. The French company, Aerospatiale, wants to buy de Havilland. It is prepared to invest $1 billion in research and development, but it wants the government to pay for a substantial part of that investment. The Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade has said that funding will have to come out of existing programs. The head of the Aerospace Industries Association of Canada has said that the existing budget is already spread too thin, and it has been reduced by some 25 per cent in the past three or four years.
Where will the money come from? The minister of industry has said that there are no additional funds. It is clear that without additional government investment, we will not have research and development in Canada.
A 1986 study by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association demonstrated that when it comes to non-tax support for research and development, Canada is not in the same league as many of our competitors. It is not a question of ownership.
Pratt & Whitney in Montreal is a foreign-owned company and yet it is one of the most research intensive companies in Canada. We will find that it has entered into a number of memoranda of understanding with the government in which the government funds a good portion of its R and D. This is the same as every other country, whether we are talking about the United States, Japan, Germany, the Scandinavian countries or France.
I will call it one o'clock and I guess resume after three o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I want to set the record straight. On Thesday, the Minister of Agriculture led this House to believe that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture was in support of opening the Canadian border to U.S. wheat. This is not true. speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the parliamentary break the American network ABC aired a 20/20 program that dealt with the case of one Charles Ng who is wanted in California to face charges in connection with a series of brutal slayings five years ago.
Mr. Ng is currently appealing his extradition to the U.S. from Canada.
The program was called "Refuge for Murderers" and that, unfortunately, is the way many Americans have come to view our country. It is embarrassing, frustrating and downright frightening the number of times that America's most wanted are shown on television and then subsequently found in Canada.
We cannot allow Canada to become a refuge for criminals. We need changes to our extradition act and we need them now.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Achilles heel of Canadian competitiveness is R and D. When the World Competitiveness Report looked at Canada, it saw that we spend a mere 1.3 per cent of GNP on science and ranked us sixteenth among our competitors.
When 400 elite policy-makers, many of them federal bureaucrats, were surveyed, they said our lack of R and D, the high dollar and high interest rates were self-inflicted wounds. They know that R and D is the key to the new products and processes that create jobs.
But the Prime Minister consistently ignores his own advisory board on science and technology when it asks him to live up to his 1984 promise to double Canadian R and D. So when the throne speech cites targets for education and training, but omits any mention whatsoever of research and development, it is dramatically significant and tragically clear. After seven years of jawboning, we will have no public policy to achieve targets for Canadian research and development. The implied policy of the Department of Finance has now become the explicit policy of the Department of Industry, Science, Technology and International Trade.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those who want Canada to survive in its present form are searching for those things we have in common. Those who think they will profit from the failure of Canada are underlining what divides us into regions and along the lines of language and culture, but there is one group of Canadians who have made the ultimate gesture in support of this great thing we call Canada. It is a group of men and women who actually fought in the name of this country in world wars, Korean conflicts, and the gulf conflict as well.
I rise today to salute them and the Royal Canadian Legion, which has mounted a public campaign in the name of national unity. The Legion realizes well that this goes beyond the bounds of partisan politics, and is taking the initiative in reminding us all of what is at stake.
May 16, 1991

The Legion has been a supporter of a strong central government in the past. But the Legion also knows that changing times demand changing attitudes. When the question is put whether Canada can change or must fragment, the Legion's answer is clear: we must change.
I would ask all those Canadians who are busy building walls in this country, walls to keep their own intolerance strong, to look toward the Legion. There is the real vision of Canada.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the plight of former Route Canada employees continues five years after the government sold this trucking company to a man who could not even get a credit card.
Two thousand workers were left without jobs. Creditors lost $60 million. Many former employees lives were shattered when they lost their homes, their livelihoods and their dignity.
Still the government refuses to launch an investigation into this dirty deal. The RCMP has been investigating the case for almost three years. Surely it has some answers by now.
Canadian taxpayers and former employees have a right to know what the RCMP has discovered.
Right now there are hundreds more truckers outside our door who understand what former Route Canada employees have been living through. They feel betrayed and sacrificed by this government to the interests of big business.
I call on the government today to show some compassion for compensating these former employees of Route Canada, to launch an investigation into its sale and to bring forward the RCMP investigation.

speakerposition: subtopic

Mr. Speaker, the elimination of interprovincial trade barriers
is a goal of this government. Why? Trade barriers within Canada make us less competitive, thus costing Canadians jobs and opportunities.
For example, in the field of agriculture, there are 167 regulations. The European Community, with 12 nations, is more open in terms of agricultural trade than we are within a single country.
The existing system rewards inefficiencies.

I believe that the creation of a single Canadian market goes hand-in-hand with national unity because it is by working together that we build a stronger more prosperous Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to introduce to all members a new commentary in the House of Commons entitled the Cross-Border Report.
The Cross-Border Report will not be convoluted or multi-topical. Rather, it will focus on one issue; crossborder shopping. Yet, I know that all members will find the report of interest. It is at the front line of our efforts to be competitive.
Cross-border shopping is a multi-faceted phenomenon dealing essentially with why the Canadian consumer finds an incentive to shop in the United States.
The exodus is fostered by a number of motivational factors, including the strength of the Canadian dollar, differences in distribution channels and mark-ups between our countries, the non-collection of provincial sales tax and the applicable duty and taxes at the border. There is aggressive U.S. marketing and advertising, as well as a free trade mentality luring the Canadian consumer. The means to address these factors lies not with one but a number of players, including all three levels of government, business and labour.
Stay tuned for the next edition in a series of many of the Cross-Border Report.

The minister of immigration is the one who is responsible for people coming into the country. I instituted an inquiry within my department. I stand by that and I think that is what responsible ministers do do; they ascertain the facts before they start spreading rumours around.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, responsible ministers know what is going on in their departments. Canadians find it unbelievable that three ministers of the Crown were kept in the dark for months before they were told that the Iraqi ambassador to Washington was seeking permission to enter Canada as a landed immigrant.
We are pleased that an inquiry will take place, and we accept the undertaking of the Prime Minister that the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, the former Minister of Employment and Immigration and the former Solicitor General will be appearing before the committee to give evidence.
I would also like the Prime Minister to give his undertaking that Mr. Raymond Chretien, Mr. David Daubney, Mr. Paul Tellier and Mr. Reid Morden will also appear before the committee to defend themselves. If the government is truly interested in getting to the truth of this matter then it will have all relevant witnesses appear before the committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have thought that the hon. member would have known by now what is the responsibility of committees of this House and their chairmen. It is up to the committee to invite whomever it wants to have appear before the committee.
I have made a commitment that those of us who are involved will appear before this committee. That is a committee matter.

The committee can invite the Queen, but that does not mean she is going to appear. I would like an undertaking from the Prime Minister to have the civil servants who were directly involved in this matter to appear before the committee.
If the Prime Minister refuses, the only conclusion we can draw is that the government really is not interested in getting to the truth of the matter. Have these officials appear so they can defend themselves against the accusations made by their political bosses.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's problem is that he has nowhere to go now that we have said that people will appear before a committee.

The court also struck down the September 14,1987 backroom deal between the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Alcan, which is the basis upon which construction of this immense project is now proceeding.
I would like to ask the Minister of the Environment to assure this House that a panel will be set up immediately and that he will assure all Canadians that all major projects from this point on will undergo an environmental assessment before they proceed, not after construction begins?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand the ruling that my friend from Skeena refers to came out this morning. I think it would only be a normal course of action for us to look at it and then act accordingly.

Oral Questions
I would like to ask the Minister of the Environment if he could assure this House that all major projects from this point on will undergo an assessment first and will he immediately set up a panel to look into Alcan's Kemano 2 project?

In the throne speech, we heard that our government is committed to increasing the number of high school graduates, cutting the illiteracy rate, increasing the amount of employee training, as well as increasing post-secondary graduates in math, science and engineering.
Can the minister apprise this House what our government is doing to increase the number of graduates in the fields of math, science and engineering?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the cornerstones of our efforts to increase the number of students in math, science and engineering is, of course, the Canada Scholarship Program which was announced by the Prime Minister in
1988.	Under that program, 9,000 scholarships have been issued to students from high school into first year in these particular subjects.
As well, we have a number of programs. The latest one, announced by the Council of Science and Technology Ministers of Canada just last week was "Innovators in the School". We expect by August of this year to have every part of this country involved in sending scientists and engineers into all of the public and high schools to talk about careers in those particular subjects.

May 16, 1991
Business of the House
I would hope that by the time this program is finished we will have some 25,000 people, qualified scientists and engineers, moving into the schools to talk about that particular issue.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
One of my constituents, Mr. Sadhu Singh, died 18 days ago. His sister, now in India, wishes to attend the funeral but was denied a visitor's visa, apparently for fear she would not return, even though her husband and two children are not joining her at the funeral.
My repeated representations to the minister's office and the minister himself have failed to move them.
Could the minister explain to this House how Mo-hamed Al-Mashat, spokesman for a murderer, can be hastily ushered into Canada as a landed immigrant, while this grieving woman is refused a visitor's visa to see her brother one last time?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I share the hon. member's preoccupation with his constituent. It is true that the hon. member has made representations. An official of this government, posted in the country in question, has refused a visitor's visa for this women. Upon receiving the representation of the hon. member, I placed an immediate inquiry to the post overseas in order that I be informed as to why this has happened. Surely, I cannot overrule an official in the Public Service-
Oh, oh.
That is outrageous.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
May I can complete my answer, Mr. Speaker.
The reason is that I cannot interfere with the decision of the public officials unless and until I know why he was refused. The minute I receive this information-and we have conveyed that to the hon. member-and know why he was refused, I can exercise my discretion and authorize that person to come to Canada for the funeral in question.
Mr. Speaker, it has been more than a week since I made my representation to the minister.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That may very well have been, but I would ask the hon. member, given the time, to put the question directly to the minister, please.

Mr. Speaker, the body of Mr. Singh cannot wait for three more weeks in a Winnipeg funeral home. Neither his sister nor the Singh family can wait and grieve indefinitely.
Where is the heart of this minister? I ask him to act now. Issue a permit, Mr. Minister.

He was not even able to give me the name, the date of birth, or address of the person we want.
Oh, oh.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to earlier questions about whether questions are out of order, I make the point that Section 359 of Beauchesne's fifth edition, which lays out what questions should be or should not be says:
(2)	The question must be brief. A preamble need not exceed one carefully drawn sentence.
(3)	The question ought to seek information and, therefore, cannot be based on a hypothesis, cannot seek an opinion, either legal or otherwise, and must not suggest its own answer, be argumentative or make representations.
I quite understand the difficulty in enforcing these strictures in Beauchesne, in that after they are made cannot be retracted. In the age of television and so on, they are out. Therefore, it is fair and appropriate that the ministry reply to the accusations, innuendo and so on that are contained in the preambles.
The point I would make is in response to a suggestion in the last session by the House leader of the Liberal Party, that Question Period be examined in terms of the length of preambles, the length of answers and the method. It is a very valid one and I am hoping that the new management committee will take this under advisement.

House leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition on the question of what is the business which is forthcoming.

order to assure everybody concerned that there is no substance whatsoever to the suggestions of impropriety about the ministry that have been laid today. We are anxious to do that. Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has said that by September the government will table its proposals for constitutional reform. The throne speech addresses the questions of unity and prosperity and I would like to quote from the throne speech:
Our unity is strengthened by a strong economy. And prosperity is enhanced by a united country.
Those are propositions that I am sure we all agree with. Does the government understand that constitutional arrangements must support our economic objectives?
Our leader, Mr. Chretien, has said that in making changes to the division of powers the essential focus must be an arrangement which best serves the needs of people, not governments or bureaucrats or politicians. Any new arrangements must provide the flexibility to meet the changing demands and challenges of the future. To my knowledge, the government has yet to make a similar statement. Quite frankly, I am concerned about recent proposals to hive off various aspects of economic and social policy, such as training of workers, to the provinces. Divorcing such training from income security policies and tax policies will make it impossible to adequately address the needs of individual Canadians.
We have to be careful about placing limits on the federal spending power. Overlapping jurisdictions are inevitable in a modem and complex world. For Canada to adapt to global realities, a comprehensive and integrated plan of action will be required, one in which training, education and social assistance policies are updated and research and technology strategies are defined on a national level.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to return to the issue of national unity more particularly. I know that we in Quebec feel some disappointment following the events of recent years. The failure of the Meech Lake Accord was interpreted wrongly, I think, as a rejection of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, it is time to go beyond emotions and to analyse more objectively. Personally, I believe that we live in one of the best countries in the world.
When I get up every morning, I thank God for keeping me alive and for the privilege of living in this country.
We do not need an exhaustive analysis to understand and realize Canada's incredible advantages and assets. I am sure that everyone can give a short personal experience. I could talk about it for a long time, but I will confine myself to a small example.
I remember visiting a refugee camp on the border of Cambodia and Thailand in 1980. In that misery, Mr. Speaker, were Canadian doctors and nurses who, in
May 16, 1991

The Address
addition to their work, acted as interpreters between some Swedes, who spoke only English besides their mother tongue, and French people. That is Canada's true vocation, Mr. Speaker. With our two languages and our different cultures that make up Canada, we can indeed play an important international role.
Should we not rather take on the challenges of the world?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am of course very pleased to speak today in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is at the crossroads, not only as a political entity, but also as an economic power in North America and in the world. More than ever, we have the duty, as individuals, to decide what kind of country we want to live in and what place it should occupy on this continent as well as in the world.
Of course, national unity plays now a pivotal part in the choices facing us. It would be a mistake, Mr. Speaker, for us collectively to refuse to face up to reality at a time when it is vital to be careful to avoid delusions. All aspects of our daily life are tied to the survival of this country which, in turn, is dependant upon unity as a link between several communities and cultures.
Because of these differences and thanks to these differences, this country is probably the best equiped to ensure the prosperity and quality of life that all the people of Canada are looking for. It is the very existence of Canada as an international power that is at stake. So, I urge you to stop and think of the implications for a moment.
I urge Canadians to consider reality, their reality, setting aside the symbols, the misunderstandings and the conflicts, between the French-speaking and English-

The Address
speaking communities, between the east and the west, between native people and non-native people or between new immigrants and not so new immigrants, and answer this question: do we still want this country?
I am talking about a country with a 125-year history as a federation, whose various communities, against all odds, share the common values of peace, justice, tolerance and liberty. These values, embodied in our lifestyle and in our institutions, are what make Canada the envy of most countries in the world.
Since I came to Ottawa in 1984, I have often been confronted, as have my colleagues from Quebec, Mr. Speaker, by the problem of the two solitudes, as we call it. I also had the opportunity to discover a richer yet more complex reality. Confronted to this reality, I realized that ordinary Canadians across the country have more of less the same needs and the same aspirations.
On major issues such as the environment, economic prosperity, the family and health, people all share the ideal of a better life, whether they live in Roberval, Quebec, or in Vegreville, Alberta. We could probably build a lot on these sound aspirations that we all share, provided we are careful, we listen and reach out.

Canada is facing formidable challenges at this time. The identity crisis our country is going through at this time raises certain basic questions which involve each and every one of us. We can blame the government but this crisis needs to be seen as the culmination of a long series of missed opportunities and broken down communications.
Often we fail to ask the real question for fear of getting real answers, the real truth.
Are we perhaps afraid of finding out what we have really become? Any identity crisis, and ours is complicated by also being a unity crisis, is a mirror into which it takes courage to look. The crisis we are experiencing contains the seeds for major change, potential rebirth of our entire country. I want to see this country have the audacity, the daring to question every aspect of this issue, to believe in its own ability to find the right answers.
I have spoken of change and rebirth. What will this consist of? It is not solely up to the government or governments to decide. All Canadians must take part in defining their country, regardless of what that definition may turn out to be. Canadians are the ones who built this country, who made it a country, and they are the ones responsible for its prosperity.
Today's men and women receive this country as an heritage from those who have gone before them. They are therefore the ones who need to be asked what future they want to see for this country.

Mr. Speaker, make no mistake. There is no cut and dried solution to the present crisis in this country. Our government has taken and will continue to take initiatives to advance the cause of national unity, but without the participation of the Canadian people and the co-operation of all major groups in Canadian society, the process is doomed to failure.
Mr. Speaker, we are not talking about another government project. We are talking about the future and the unity of this country. Elow could we agree on a plan for the future to renew our unity, without calling on the partnership of all Canada's dynamic forces? Without this kind of participation, we will never be receptive to the problems of others. Since there seems to be a consensus in this country on changing the status quo, perhaps it is time to get down to basics and talk about foundations for a new union.
Canada will deserve to be called a country if it has a minimum of consensus. Only broad participation by Canadians can guarantee that a consensus will be reached. We are embarking on an exercise in reflection that will not be complete until Canadians have stated what they want the future of this country to be.
During the months to come, Canadians will have to think about this country's future. We will have to start by thinking about what we are and the kind of society we have built over the years.
As the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I can testify to major achievements by Canadian men and women, and I also want to do so as an individual who is concerned about the quality of life of his fellow citizens and who welcomes this responsibility.
In the field of health and welfare, Canada, during the past 50 years, has adopted policies and programs that are the envy of practically everyone. In the heat of the
May 16, 1991

debate on free trade and again today, when we are discussing the pressures of international competition, Canada has vigorously renewed its commitments. Despite frequently expressed concerns about the intentions of our government, we have not only maintained our commitments, we have improved on them.
Mr. Speaker, Canada's health care system is recognized as one of the best in the world. Wherever they are in this country, Canadians can be assured of receiving high quality services. They can depend on a national system whose excellence owes a great deal to cooperation among the provinces and to provincial initiatives to improve that system. Because of needs and expectations, the health care sector has expanded enormously over the years. Mr. Speaker, the federal and provincial governments spend $40 billion of their revenue on health care, out of a total of 60 billion.
This year, the federal government transfered $14 billion to the provinces in the form of transfer payments and tax points.

It is more important than ever that the main principles that have served and continue to serve as the foundation of our health system be reaffirmed. I can state without hesitation that features that make our system unique- universality and accessibility-will not be challenged in any way. The risk that those people who are most vulnerable might have to bear the consequences of any change of that kind has convinced me of the need to reaffirm that our national standards will remain intact.
In a time of limited financial resources and increasing pressures on our provincial health services, the federal government is prepared to intensify its co-operation with the provinces. We must find ways of helping our health systems respond more effectively to pressures resulting from such factors as demographic change, technological development and public expectations.
It is also the responsibility of the federal government to ensure that our native people have the greatest possible accessibility to health and social services. This responsibility which the federal government has assumed on behalf of the people of Canada for nearly 125 years
The Address
has contributed to the establishment of an extensive system of facilities and services for the native and Inuit population extending from the Yukon to the maritime provinces, a system which today consists of some 488 health service facilities including nine hospitals in eight large regions.
Through this system we are able to help the various communities in their efforts to decrease alcohol and drug consumption on reserves, thereby helping to reduce family violence.

Mr. Speaker, this fact demonstrates the importance of having a national vision of health and welfare that covers the needs of all communities in this country.
The protection of public health is another area whose impact is impressive. Every day, the lives of every one of us are in some way affected by action taken by the Health Protection Branch of Health and Welfare Canada: monitoring the processing and manufacturing of food and drugs, monitoring medical products compliance, taking part in investigations of epidemics, analysing drug samples as part of the Canadian drugs strategy, and so forth. The expectations of Canadians in this area are very high. It is a difficult task that requires many resources and action on a national scale.

Another area in which the activities of the federal government influence the day-to-day reality of Canadians is the area of social programs. It is important to know that Canadians are proud of their image as a caring nation. As our country has matured, social programs have grown and changed to better meet our evolving needs. Although we hold different ideas about the best way to help needy Canadians, the shared value of caring for each other unifies us across the country, and in all regions we expect governments to have a social face.
It is in keeping with these values that we must take stock of the future. Our achievements are considerable but there are challenges which remain. No government program can or should replace the family. However, where governments can assist is by helping the family respond to changing needs and by creating a healthy environment in which Canadian children can live, learn and grow.

The Address
More than ever Canadian women are joining the labour force. Sometimes this is a choice, but more often than not it is an economic necessity. At the same time as holding down jobs, many parents must take care of children and elderly parents. Lone parents face a unique challenge in working while trying to provide the best care for their children. The many roles that family members must play create a tremendous strain. As the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I am pleased that the throne speech promises a review of policies in relation to the family. I want to ensure that our policies best meet the present and future needs of families.
Our most precious resource is our children. By their very nature, children belong to society's most vulnerable group. Modem society, for all its technological achievements and advances, has not done well enough with the children. In our country, children have a problem which we cannot ignore; as well as assisting families, we must continually help children out of poverty. While we have seen some improvement in child poverty rates, we must continue to seek the fuller understanding of the root causes of poverty, and work with other governments and voluntary organizations to find effective ways to keep children out of the welfare trap.
The Children's Bureau will help me to develop recommendations to cabinet to fulfil the commitments made at the summit. I envision Canada's National Action Plan as addressing a broad range of issues which affect children, including enforcement of child support orders and action against child pornography.

Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I have to mention the government effort to fight AIDS. We developed a national strategy, which has the support of community groups, non-government agencies and all levels of government, a remarkable achievement in terms of consultation and partnership.
Let me assure you that I will cany the work initiated by my predecessor in that field. Therefore I undertake to step up all joint efforts which will help us beat this horrible virus.
Mr. Speaker, we are facing other great challenges. Canadian men and women expect their government to
use extreme caution, and it is vital that we live up to then-expectations. Canada has a good name, thanks to its vision based on such values as fairness, compassion, tolerance and generosity. As a nation, we now need to re-affirm our unanimity cohesion in the values and the assets we share. Health and social programs are some of our vital assets.
That is what I want achieve both as a minister and a member of this government. I came to Ottawa hoping I could contribute to Canada's growth, bearing in mind the values, principles and differences which make our country. I hope we can soon find the path to unity, so that we cany on with this humna-scale undertaking.
I invite everyone to take an active part in the preservation of our heritage, since, in light of the challenge that lies ahead, we can hope for even better tomorrows.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for giving me the opportunity to make a few remarks and also to direct a question to the minister of health.
Just this very day there was a very grim report put out by a journalist from the Edmonton Journal. Basically what that article says is that northerners lead the nation in most classes of illness. It says:
With the exception of heart disease, Canada's northern territories experience higher death and disease rates than the rest of the country. Birth and infant mortality rates are also higher.
It also quotes the minister of health from the Northwest Territories:
It is only recently that we have been able to supply a fairly decent level of water and sewage, says Nellie Coumoyea, the Territorial Health Minister.
It goes on to say that it is not unusual to have as many as 16 people living in a poorly ventilated, substandard home. The chronic housing shortage is a major obstacle to combating infectious diseases, such as tuberculosis and respiratory infections. Coumoyea adds that an additional 2,000 housing units are needed to meet current demands, never mind the nightmare of an anticipated population explosion that could see the vast region's population double within 30 years.
May 16, 1991

Housing is the number one health priority in the Northwest Territories and the second priority is environmental health in the homes, says Dr. Paul Cappon of McGill University.
They go on to say, and this is very important, that a 1986 survey showed that 77 per cent of Inuit women and 65 per cent of Dene and Metis women smoke, giving women in the territories a cancer rate four times higher than the rest of Canada. More than half the residents of the Northwest Territories and 40 per cent of Yukoners smoke, compared to one third of the population nationally.
This is a very grim indictment and I would like to get some kind of an indication from the minister of health. I know he is new to his portfolio, but in what way can we as parliamentarians and elected officials, in a responsible and non-partisan manner, try to grapple with these very, very difficult health issues that affect the remote areas of Canada?
In 1991, should we expect to have diseases that were unheard of and that were rampant in the 1940s and 1950s, such as tuberculosis?

I have two bands in my riding and the highest rate of suicide in Lac-Saint-Jean is in Point Bleue, in the Montagnais band in my riding.
I hope that my colleague will agree with me that there are many factors dealing with the problems, particularly with these people. I am not sure that as a country we have always given those people the chance to get out of those problems in the same efficient way we gave to it other people. That is why I have particularly asked the department to look at means that could be used to increase help given, particularly to northern bands.
The Address
I was in Winnipeg last Saturday. The first visit I made as the minister of health was to the office in Winnipeg, committing myself to return and to particularly meet with native people to see what we can do better. Already the drug strategy and family violence have been approached, as well as child intervention, and we will have more on that in the fall. I will keep that in mind. It is veiy sensitive.
It is not just a matter of saying we will, it is a matter of seeing the ways and means we have. Resources are more scarce than they were, but I committed myself to do my best to help those people the best we can.
