speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank you for recognizing me at this time, in the midst of a debate which surely will count in the history of Canada and will probably become more acrimonious in the months to come. I have in mind in particular the speech from the minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs this morning in which he told us that they would be introducing a bill on the holding of referenda when we know that a similar measure has been introduced in the National Assembly in Quebec City and should become law before the end of June.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, we are in a pre-referendum period. Therefore, coming here to tell our Englishspeaking colleagues what we want and what the situation is, is fulfilling the role the Bloc Quebecois sets for itself, the role of being a link with English Canada at a time when the concept of sovereignty is more and more accepted and is becoming a political necessity.
In the next few minutes, Mr. Speaker, I would like to convince you that sovereignty is also an economic necessity. Naturally, over the last twelve months we have seen a lot of water flow under the bridge. After the failure of
The Address
the Meech Lake Accord, Quebec had extensive studies done on its future.
I think that all members of this House will agree that the Belanger-Campeau commission was a model of democracy, a model of broadening political horizons, not only for the elected members of the National Assembly but also for the leaders of various communities and groups in Quebec. Besides, it was an unprecedented experience in Canada, where for the first time non-elected people were part of such a broad, wide-ranging, important process.
There was also the Allaire Report in the Quebec Liberal Party, which was adopted by a large majority. So to those who claim that sovereignty is advocated only by a minority or who think that only independence crusaders believe in it, I want to tell them that the consensus in Quebec is growing day by day and since the failure of Meech Lake, we have learned not to trust others but to decide on our collective future ourselves.
That is why when I see federal initiatives that may be intended to counter the initiatives of the Government of Quebec, I tell them that they are really pale imitations.
For example, we have seen the Spicer commission in recent months. I feel sorry for English Canada to have to go through this charade instead of discussing and really looking into the kind of country you want. Of course, the Beaudoin-Edwards committee has been concerned with the mechanics, but completely ignored the substance, the content. And God knows that in Canada now, the two confronting visions have nothing to do with process: they are realities in people's hearts and minds. And whatever process is adopted, do not think that you can reconcile the difference between a group that wants a strong central government-and I respect those in English Canada who want a strong central government; it is their right. For others, the only real government that counts is the one that controls the majority, the one in the National Assembly.
No travelling committee, not one, two, three or twelve committees will change the reality out there. The debate now going on in this country is not one of process, but of vision. Everything hinges on there being two visions but only one country. What is missing is a country. That is why we see more and more Quebecers who traditionally

May 16, 1991
The Address
rejected sovereignty come to realize that the differences are irreconcilable. We tried everything.
The Minister of Health asked us earlier what kind of country we wanted. Quebecers have unequivocally answered this question twice already and, each time, their cry from the heart was not heard. No wonder that a formation like the Bloc Quebecois was established. No wonder that a formation like the Reform Party is emerging today. This is happening because of the fundamental difference between the legal vision of Canada that you are proposing and what this country is really about. All the difference is there.
It is about the real country that we want to talk about in this House, Mr. Speaker. We know it offends the pure and innocent ears of some of our hon. colleagues. We know this is not the traditional argument heard in this House where efforts are made to disguise reality by pretending that the country depicted in the legislation corresponds to the real Canada. However, the reality that people see in their heads and in their hearts is totally different.
The reason why traditional parties are facing massive rejection throughout the country is very simple: they do not suit the real country and the aspirations of the people who live in this real country, outside of this ivory tower we live in, here, in Ottawa.
So, when I hear the Speech from the Throne challenge, call upon the Canadian people to participate, the first question that comes to mind, Mr. Speaker, is who is going to believe this government? It is the first one that comes to mind in response to this challenge. For then-part, Canadians would like to challenge this government to run again in an election. In that way, this Speech from the Throne is fraudulent. It was made by an illegitimate government, a fact corroborated by all public opinion polls. This government would do the country a big favour if the Prime Minister were to decide to put Canada's interest before that of his own party and to ask Canadians and Quebecers to pick true representative in these times of turmoil. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the make-up of this Parliament would reflect the actual make-up of this country and not that of some dream that this Speech from the Throne is trying to sell us.
We know what the reality is in fact. So, when our friends opposite claim they will take up these great challenges, we know that they lack the moral authority as well as the capacbility and the will to do so. We know they are the lowest ever in the polls: they have lost the trust of just about everybody in Canada.

Under this government, which is allegedly so generous and so perfect, as we speak and while the Prime Minister is praising the great virtues of federalism, 11,180 banckruptcies have been recorded in Canada over the past year. At a time when the economic policies of the government should be one fostering a strong economy, as promised in its last Speech from the Throne, interest rates are oscillating between 10 and 12 percent, while our dollar is at 87 cents.
So, we talk about sovereignty, Mr. Speaker, it is not strictly a matter of political necessity. Sovereignty is increasingly becoming an economic necessity, and that statement is not from me. Even the Quebec Chamber of Commerce tells us, in its brief, that it is time to act. They say the decision-making process should be put in place immediately. The same recommendation was made to the Quebec government by the Belanger-Campeau commission. That is what the legislation the Quebec government introduced yesterday is about, one more step toward a referendum in Quebec.
But, this afternoon, the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs told us that the federal government will want to hold its own referendum. They will introduce their own referendum legislation in an attempt to weaken the resolve of Quebecers and create a diversion.
Mr. Speaker, we realize this is an attempt to create a diversion! So we invite all those who want to relive the torments of conscription to hold their federal referendum; we invite them to ask Quebecers the real question and they will get an answer they never hoped for.
Mr. Speaker, to those who thought they could, out of Ottawa, scare the Quebec people with their jackboots, I say: Go pay a visit to Quebecers in the next little while, you will see how low your credibility level is, how you will
May 16, 1991

not be able to convince anyone, because the onus of proof rests with you, and so far you have not delivered.

In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, there is a difference between these two issues.
It is my duty, as a member of the Opposition, to make the government accountable. I do not apologize for it: That is the reason why I was sent here by my constituents. The people of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell have asked me to represent them; they have given me a mandate to represent them in this House. Because of circumstances, because of what has happened in the other 294 ridings in Canada, I sit on the Opposition side. It is not because of what happened in my own riding, indeed, if I had not been elected, I simply would not be here. I am on the Opposition side because of what has happened in the other ridings. You are either a member of the Opposition or a member of the government. As a member of the government, one tries, as best as possible, to conduct the affairs of the country, like any other government in the past. But as a member of the Opposition, one has to make the government accountable.
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member says that the government lacks credibility, I can certainly share his
opinion; however, Mr. Speaker, that does not mean that Canada lacks credibility. It may be true that unemployment is high in Canada and that our monetary policy is not good, and it is an opinion that I share, but that does not mean that Canada is a bad country. Those are the fundamental differences on the basis of which we must separate our role as spokespersons in the House of Commons from our reactions toward those who govern and those who form the opposition. But this role does not allow us to say to Canadians that their country does not work because people have lost confidence in those who are in power.

It might not be fashionable for a member of the Opposition to formulate such wishes, but I think that in doing so, Mr. Speaker, I am not wishing that the government opposite run the economy the way they did in the past, but that the minister succeed in keeping our country together, because that principle is larger than I, larger than the members opposite and even larger, with all due respect, than the occupant of the Chair. because I want our country to remain strong, united and prosperous in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, could I ask the consent of the House to the New Democratic Party's intention to split our speeches into two speeches of 10 minutes with five minutes of questions from now on. I do not think that should be any problem.
I would like to begin my comments on the Speech from the Throne with some general comments. The speech begins by talking about Canada's history as a history of builders and achievers and how Canadian men and women created a society that is as free and fair as any on earth. I want to make sure that the government was not intending to include itself in this category of builders and achievers and creators of a free and fair society. I assure the government that the people of Canada do not share the view that this government is in that category and sees the government as a destroyer and creator of something which is unfair, not something which is fair.
The speech goes on to talk about the need to rebuild Canadian unity and overcome the acrimony, apathy and incomprehension that exists. Of course we all agree with that, but the government must also take its responsibility as one of the main culprits in generating disunity,

May 16, 1991
The Address
acrimony, apathy and incomprehension about the importance of Canada and holding the country together.
The Speech from the Throne goes on to talk about putting Canada first and wanting all parliamentarians to put Canada first, to set partisan motives aside and work for a stronger country.
How can the government expect us to put all our partisan views aside? How can it expect us to buy into its view of Canada which has generated such unemployment, such misery and such poverty across this country? The government is not learning from its mistakes. The New Democratic Party cannot participate in working towards the sort of Canada that this government wants. We will, of course, work towards a Canada which is one and united, but a Canada which is fair, compassionate and cares about people rather than corporations.
Even in the Speech from the Throne, there is more of the same. There are more of the government's economic policies, which have tom the country apart, being proposed for the next session of Parliament. There is more privatization, more deregulation, and more economic policies which will tear the country apart. There are more references to cuts to transfer payments which will tear the country apart in terms of our social policies. This is a trend which has been going on for quite some time.
The Speech from the Throne talks about a Constitution that will unite a nation. Well, so it should, but so should a government unite a nation. It should seek compromise and consensus, not just at the time when a Constitution is being framed, not just when a Constitution is being negotiated. It should also unite a nation at times when we are dealing with social policies and economic policies.
We have seen the tragedy of this government's economic policies. Social programs have been cut at a time when they are needed most. We have seen this tragedy caused by the free trade agreement, by unfair taxation, by the high dollar, by high interest rates, by cuts in transfer payments to the provinces, by deregulation, by privatization and by cuts to national institutions like CBC and VIA Rail.
In spite of all the evidence this direction is continued in the throne speech. We have free trade for provinces
too. This means the end of manufacturing industries in Saskatchewan. It means the concentration of more manufacturing in central Canada and Ontario, away from the hinterland economies. It means more job losses, more pain, more poverty, more unemployment and more sickness in the regions. This is thoroughly unacceptable to the people of Saskatchewan, thoroughly unacceptable to the people of Atlantic Canada and all the regions of Canada who have not received a fair deal under this or, indeed, former governments.
There is much that could be said about the general thrust of the Speech from the Throne but I would like to concentrate on one issue which is not in the throne speech but which should have been. It deals with matters of poverty and, in particular, child poverty. We all remember that this House, this government committed itself to removing child poverty by the year 2000.
We need a plan and a timetable to ensure that child poverty is eliminated by the year 2000.
The government in the throne speech has committed itself to implement the commitments made. This would take a major change in attitude. Somebody must have been on the road to Damascus to see some revelation which would suggest that we have to do something different. Yet this government has been a government which has slashed education programs and slashed transfer payments to the provinces for social programs in B.C., Alberta, and Ontario. This has had major negative implications on children, yet now it wants to say that it is going to change for the better and that it will ensure that Canadian girls and boys will be better educated, better protected and better nurtured. If they are going to be better protected, it seems to me they had better be protected from the present Government of Canada which has caused them great harm over the last short while.
I would like to make two brief comments with regard to the children's summit which is mentioned in the throne speech. The government talks about following through on those commitments.
There are two commitments in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. One is to ensure that children enjoy the highest attainable standard of

health and facilities for treatment of illness and rehabilitation of health-the highest attainable standards.
Anybody in this country knows that we are far, far away from ensuring that children across this country, particularly those in rural and northern areas and poor children, receive the highest attainable standard of health. They do not, and it is time the government made some commitments in that regard.
In addition, with regard to education, there is a commitment to ensure that higher education be accessible to all on the basis of capacity, by every appropriate means. Yet this government has slashed funding to higher education which has meant less and less successful education for low and middle income Canadians, higher tuition fees, and so on. We can see that all across the country in our own universities and our own communities where tuition fees are going through the roof.
What we need is not more rhetoric. We need to be caring about children. We need policy initiatives which actually resolve the problem.
We need aggressive action on pay equity. We need an end to tax loopholes that benefit the wealthy individuals and corporations in our society. We need to cut subsidies to the rich corporations instead of slashing social programs for those who need it most. We need a national child care strategy. This is the first Speech from the Throne for a long time with not even a mention of child care.
We need viable housing initiatives. We need increased social assistance levels to protect those who are weakest in our society. We need to reverse cutbacks to health and post-secondary education. We need to be paying attention to aboriginal and minority concerns so that the poverty gap between those groups and other Canadians can be bridged.
These things were not in the speech. There was no commitment to addressing the real concerns of Canadians or addressing the real concerns of those least affluent Canadians. That is what we needed. Instead, we received more of the same disastrous policies which we have seen over the last few years.
In closing, Canadians need and Canadians demand better policies.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened to the throne speech earlier this week and looked to the government to provide the Canadian people with a plan for economic recovery, a plan for a statement on national unity and the Constitution and, sadly, we were all very disappointed. It seems to be again the same, tired old Tory agenda, an agenda that has brought us the free trade deal, an agenda that has cost Canadians thousands and thousands of jobs in every region of this country, an agenda that has increased taxes, increased the burden on to the backs of middle and lower income people and an agenda that has failed to this point on national unity.
National unity is much more than which spending powers are administered by which level of government. It is about a nation in which individuals are secure, employed and contribute to the good of all in our society. It is about a nation in which every Canadian is valued regardless of the region they come from, the colour of their skin, or their abilities.
Canadians do want a strong Canada, a diverse and a vibrant nation, one they can be proud of. I have spoken to my constituents, as many of the people in this House have spoken to their constituents, and have listened to their concerns on the future of this country and on the
pain and the worry they are feeling right now about the very future of our nation.
It is hard to be optimistic about Canada when you are under attack by your own government, a government that has brought us the GST, brought us the free trade deal, brought cutbacks, one that put capping on the Canada Assistance Plan to Ontario, to British Columbia, to Alberta, and one that implemented cutbacks to social programs and left Canadians feeling very disintegrated and worried about the future.
Many Canadians are feeling the impact of the trade deal, particularly in the province of Ontario. It is not just Ontario, however, that is losing manufacturing jobs. In my own riding of New Westminster, there is a plant which has been making steel tubing for 33 years under Canadian ownership, providing jobs in my community. It had been purchased by an American firm recently, and within three months that company, Wolverine, is moving south of the border, closing that plant in Canada. It seems that what the Americans got out of the trade deal is a market in Canada but no commitment to jobs in Canada. Our government gave away that commitment to jobs; 180 jobs were lost in a very small community. That is just one example of what is happening right across this country.
We have seen it with the truckers who are out here today and have been here all week demonstrating. They were demonstrating a year ago about deregulation and about the changes in their industry. They were warning the government in saying that the government's initiatives in deregulation were bad for them and bad for their industry.
The government does not listen. It continues along the same blind policies, policies that are really ruining our country and ruining the sense of people in the nation as Canadians. I wonder which jobs are next on the government's hit list.
I listened to the throne speech for any mention of the green plan that was unveiled by this government with a great deal of attention, hoopla and promises, but it was not mentioned. The commitments of the green plan are not being fulfilled at all. The Fraser River runs right through both parts of my riding-Burnaby and New Westminster. There was a commitment in the green plan for action on the Fraser River. That river is one of the
May 16, 1991

lifeblood rivers of the province of British Columbia, and where is the action to clean up that river?
What have the members of the government done with the green plan so far? They have spent $37,000 to test the reaction on a logo. They spent $12,000 on picture frames. They spent $150,000 on communications advice from private firms. They have spent almost $2 million on advertising. What has been done on the Fraser so far? They say it is coming; when is it coming? People are waiting in every region of British Columbia. People in their ridings are asking questions and people in my riding are asking questions. They say soon. People have been asking the questions for seven years of your government and have got no response on the issue of the Fraser River.
That river is important in British Columbia for tourism, fishing and for the lumber industry, and the member opposite knows that. It is of major importance in our province. We keep hearing that there is going to be an announcement but it never comes. I have constituents calling me weekly about when that announcement is coming. They get no answer from the Department of the Environment of this government.
I was pleased about the throne speech mentioning a blue ribbon panel on violence against women. I am also concerned that this new committee has precluded immediate action on gender sensitivity training for judges. I am concerned that the government is ignoring one simple and effective action on violence against women, and that is to remove the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan, which funds shelters for battered women, child care and social assistance. Abused women must have the support they need. They need a sympathetic justice system and they need economic options.
Nobody knows what a blue ribbon panel is. It sounds like some kind of prize at an agricultural fair. We have had experience with this government's blue ribbon panel in the past: the De Grandpre blue ribbon panel. Most of us will remember what Canadians got from that blue ribbon panel.
I am concerned that the present panel may preclude a royal commission on violence against women, which, if it were implemented, like the 1970 royal commission on
The Address
the status of women, would have focused public attention on the issue, raised awareness, provided education and led to government and public action on this issue.
I hope that the panel will be made up of victims of violence, those who work in the front lines with victims of violence, and women-positive researchers. I hope that this panel hears from women and issues a definitive report which is taken seriously by this government and acted upon.
There is a promise of programs for disabled people in the throne speech. I support any program that makes our society more accessible to the disabled, but I also want to alert the government to the fact that disabled women are at a far greater risk of violence and attack.
I would like the government to keep the particular problems of disabled women in mind when it sets up these programs for the disabled and when it sets up the panel on violence against women.
Except for the panel and the programs for the disabled, which account for three sentences in the throne speech, the speech was a disappointment to Canadian women. There was no mention of child care. It was promised in 1984 and 1988. It was mentioned in every other throne speech, but not even mentioned this time.
As of March 1990, there were 433,000 children under the age of three with no parents at home to care for them. As of March 1990, there were 47,000 day care spaces, including family day care, for children of that age. That leaves almost 387,000 children under the age of three with informal, insecure arrangements which range widely in quality, or with no child care services at all.
There is no commitment to strengthen the employment equity legislation which comes up for renewal this year. There is no commitment to affordable housing. There is no commitment to remove the discrimination against immigrant women in federally employment-related language training programs.
There is no commitment to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

May 16, 1991
The Address
There is no promise of fairness for women federal Public Service employees. In the 1986 throne speech they promised to correct inequitable wage rates in the public service. Now this government is blocking the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal hearing into unfair wage rates for women in the Public Service.
The throne speech talks about literacy, education and yet, the government froze spending on education which amounts to a loss of millions of dollars in funding to education year after year.
The throne speech talks about Canada's economic strength and the most advanced social programs in the world. I do not know what world this government is talking about. Is it Mars? Here on planet earth, most western European countries have a much more advanced parental leave program and child care system than we do here in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I think you are signalling me that my time is up. I would like to make a comment about the government's request to set aside partisan comments in the House of Commons. I am happy to support the government when and if it brings in good policies for the Canadian people.
For example, I and my party did support a government Private Members' Bill to help women have access to their share of the Canada Pension Plan. This was a positive step and we all supported it.
However, do not expect me to support the GST. Do not ask me to support cuts to leave for adoptive parents. Do not ask me to support a bill that will harm the Canadian people. We want effective action from this government.

subtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have an opportunity to comment on the throne speech delivered on Monday by the Right Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn, Governor General of Canada.
As the Prime Minister eloquently expressed yesterday, Canada is at a crossroads. Regardless of the final direction and outcome, Canada will never be the same. To those who take great pride in wallowing in defeatism and pessimism about Canada's future, let me say that no generation in Canada's history has ever passed without its share of doom and gloom forecast. Despite the
naysayers, Canada has endured, more vibrant and alive with each passing year. I have never been more optimistic about our future.
Yes, it was tragic that Meech Lake died. However, that accord was carrying excess baggage not related to the Constitution.
The failure of the Meech Lake Accord has caused worry about national unity, but it also made two things clear: we must find a better way to amend the Constitution, and Canadians want to have a say in the process.
Accordingly, in November 1990, the Prime Minister announced the establishment of the Spicer commission and, in December, the formation of the special joint committee on the constitutional amending formula. Frankly, it would be naive to expect a magic formula to come from the deliberations of these bodies to cure all the aches and pains of our nationhood. However, in both cases a genuine attempt is being made to develop a national consensus rather than a provincial, territorial or special interest group perspective of Canada.
The wounds of past grievances are deep, but if we are true to our hearts and intellects, we can heal them. The risks created by our current disagreements are wide, but together we can bridge them.
That is the philosophy of the Prime Minister, the government and myself, and that is the direction expressed in the throne speech. Many Canadians blame the current problems of the economy on the Prime Minister and the policies of our government when, in very real terms, we have championed reforms and changes necessary to produce and ensure prosperity for all Canadians for years to come.
There is no denying that there has been a 2.5 per cent drop in the economy's performance, and high interest rates have contributed. However, interest rates are coming down and we must not lose sight of the fact that the U.S. economy has been in recession as well, with the resulting dampening effect on our economy.
In the current recession there has been a loss of 6.5 per cent of manufacturing jobs. However, in the recession of 1981 and 1982, the loss of manufacturing jobs was 12 per cent. Present circumstances, although undesirable, testify to the resiliency of the economy under our government's leadership. In fact, although the unemployment rate stands at 10.2 per cent, 1.285 million jobs have been created in Canada since September 1984 when
May 16, 1991

we were first elected, and 470,000 of those jobs were in Ontario alone.
Of the jobs created by the Progressive Conservative government, 76.8 per cent have been full-time employment opportunities. As a government we are fully committed to further reductions in federal spending and deficit. As outlined in the latest budget and reaffirmed in the throne speech, the deficit will be brought down to under $25 billion in 1992-93 and $6.5 billion by 1994.
From 1992 through to 1995, program spending will be limited to an average of 3 per cent a year. We practise what we preach. The provincial governments have certainly been spending on a much more lavish scale, and the same applies to municipal governments.
The bottom line is simply that if competitiveness is the key economic issue of the 1990s, Canada is off to a very rocky start this decade. Our efforts to improve Canada's economic efficiency through the free trade deal, the GST, unemployment insurance reform, spending controls and deficit reduction, have all been bitterly opposed. Much of the opposition is based on the erroneous belief in Canada that the world has changed so little in recent decades that Canada need not change in order to keep up.
Many Canadians honestly believe that our current standard of living can be maintained without adjusting to the new global economy and by using the same economic and business strategies that have proved successful in the past.
Nothing could be further from the truth. If those delusions continue to distort discussion and action on national competitiveness, it will doom Canadians to unnecessary failure.
The course outlined in the throne speech attempts to steer Canadians clear of a head-in-the-sand approach to our economic well-being.
However, the throne speech did not only dwell on questions of the Constitution and the economy, it reaffirmed our commitment to the proposition that building a prosperous economy is fully compatible with maintaining a healthy environment.
The Address
In fact, since coming to power in 1984, our government has shown decisive leadership in placing an emphasis on the state of Canada's environment.
Briefly, I would like to review a few key highlights. In the current 1991-92 fiscal year, we have committed over $1 billion to environmental programs. The Acid Rain Abatement Program initiated in February 1985 committed the seven provinces east of Saskatchewan to reducing their annual emissions of sulphur dioxide, the principle cause of acid rain, by 50 per cent of 1980 levels by 1994.
To date, sulphur dioxide emissions in Canada have been reduced by 40 per cent.
We have shown leadership with several important initiatives intended to reduce the presence of industrial toxins in our fresh water.
In October 1989 we announced a $125 million five-year Great Lakes action plan to deal with health aspects of pollution, prevent toxic contamination and start a clean-up of areas in the Great Lakes basin.
In addition, in June 1988 we announced a five-year $110 million program to protect and restore the quality of the St. Lawrence River. We have introduced some of the toughest environmental legislation in the world, including the Canadian Environmental Protection Act and the federal environmental assessment process.
However, nothing is more significant than the Canada-United States air quality accord signed by the President of the United States, George Bush, and our Prime Minister on March 13.
I have served for over 10 years on a special parliamentary committee on acid rain, and in this Parliament as a member of the Standing Committee on the Environment.
I can honestly say that this historic agreement will have a significant impact on acid rain depositions in my riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka and elsewhere for years to come.
We have only touched the tip of the iceberg in terms of the environmental initiatives and programs our government has been responsible for since 1984. In the throne speech, we reaffirmed our commitment to using the comprehensive, six-year, $3 billion green plan as the principle vehicle by which Canadians will be helped to

May 16, 1991
The Address
clean up, protect and enhance the environment over the coming months and years.
I am confident that the green plan initiatives, combined with actions by the provinces and the private sector, will ensure that Canadians have the clean air, water and land essential for a quality standard of living.
Finally, I was very happy to see that the throne speech established the family as a major priority. The family is, after all, the basic unit of Canadian society. Its strengthening should be a major objective of government policy.
I am encouraged by the fact that our government recognizes that Canadian society is changing and considerable pressure has been placed on the family unit. In light of those changes and pressures, it is reassuring that the government has made a commitment to renewing its policies to ensure that they are well tailored to meet the current and future needs of Canadian families.
The government already provides substantial funding for child care, allocating close to $1 billion annually through a number of tax and expenditure programs. Recent changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act now makes available a total of $1 billion per year to assist mothers and fathers in caring for new bom children. However, I believe we are taking a significant step in the right direction with our commitment to a national action plan for children which will address a broad range of issues including child care, enforcement of child support orders, and action against child pornography.
In the course of reviewing existing policies, it is my hope that we examine closely the family tax and support system currently in place. As it stands now, the family tax and support system is cumbersome, inefficient, and unfair in its treatment of the family. Many aspects of the present system weaken rather than strengthen the national fibre.
In concluding, let me say that in many ways Canadians are a family. True, we have our differences and have gone through our fair share of growing pains. But like a family, I believe that when push comes to shove, the time comes to pull together. We have reached that point today in Canada.
The directions laid out in the throne speech do not provide all the answers or solutions to our present
ailments. We do not even suggest that we have a cure-all. What we are doing as a government and in the commitments outlined in the throne speech is reaching out as family members across the floor of the House of Commons and across this great land, saying let us work together to ensure that a great country becomes even greater.
As individuals, as a government, as a people, we are far from being perfect, but then who is. Yet, as a nation we are the envy of the world. Indeed, Canada is a living and international ideal worth preserving and nurturing for generations to come.
The distinguished Canadian historian, A.R.M. Lower, in his book Colony to Nation made a reference to Canada which to me is quite appropriate given our present circumstances, and I quote:
In every generation Canadians have had to rework the miracle of
their political experience. Canada has been created because there has
existed within the hearts of its people a determination to build for
themselves an enduring home. Canada is a supreme act of faith.
Canadians have not lost that faith, and I have not lost that faith. For the sake of future generations, I hope the majority of the members of this House have not lost that faith either.
Mr. Speaker, again it has been a privilege to comment on the Speech from the Throne.

subtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to comment on the future plans of this government for national unity and economic prosperity, as laid out in Monday's throne speech.
In doing so, I must express my disappointment that at this time with so much concern over the state of the nation and the economy, and concern by all Canadians over the state of the nation and the economy, the speech shows no sense of direction or any evidence of the leadership that this country needs to survive and prosper as a country.
We needed action on the problem of keeping Canada together, but we have another joint committee. On the economy and competitiveness, we needed a sign from this government that it realized the disastrous effects its policies have had over the past eight years. They have not worked. Instead, we saw that it plans to stay on course.
May 16, 1991

My talk here tonight will be on these two items; the Constitution and national unity, and the lack of what I consider economic direction by this government in such a critical time of our country.
With respect to the Constitution and national unity, 11 months have passed since the Meech Lake Accord failed. In that time, our Prime Minister has appointed two commissions, the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future, otherwise known as the Spicer committee or commission, and the Special Joint Committee of the Elouse and the Senate on the Amending Process for the Canadian Constitution, otherwise known as the Beau-doin-Edwards committee of which I was a member. Both were set up to seek out the views of Canadians on what they want their country to look like in the future and how they want their Constitution changed to reflect their values, if it needs to be done.
As well, we have seen Quebec, who has had two studies, the Belanger-Campeau, a committee set up with politicians from all parties, as well as members from outside of government, interested Quebecers. We have also seen the Liberal report on Allaire. That is Quebec's combined position towards Canada and what it needs or where it wants to go within this framework of Canada.
I have to say that I regret that the provinces have not come across in the same way, but I am not sure they have been encouraged by our Prime Minister or by the Government of Canada to start looking at this very serious question.
I was a member of the Beaudoin-Edwards committee. Since February 19,1991 this committee has held about 27 public sessions both here and outside of Ottawa. We dealt with a very distinct area in the Canadian picture or in the Canadian Constitution. We dealt with the question; was there something wrong with our Constitution, with the amending formula and was there a need for a referendum or a constituent assembly. I do not really want to pre-empt the report of that committee. We have been pre-empted already by the Prime Minister who set up another committee without waiting to hear what we had to say, but we did hear from experts on this item.
I think we heard from experts across the country on our present day Constitution. Unfortunately, I can say,
The Address
in contradiction to the member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka, who thinks we should be looking for a better way to amend our Constitution, that none of the experts said it was the Constitution itself, the present day Constitution, that was so bad in the Meech Lake process, they said it was the process itself in Meech Lake that did not allow public participation.
Actually, the current Constitution has worked twice out of three times; once in 1983 and again, I think, in
1987.	It did not work in 1988. But if one looks at the Meech Lake Accord, what was it? It was a new amending formula agreed to by 10 provincial premiers and the Prime Minister. It was not even in our Constitution. Everything in the Meech Lake package, except for one item, needed unanimity.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, I made the mistake that probably most Canadians make, nothing in that package except one item needed unanimity. The rest could have been done by the seven and fifty rule in the Constitution.
I am sure most of it would have passed had there been flexibility on the part of our leaders, which I think was lacking, and public participation, so people would know exactly what our politicians were doing in the Meech Lake Accord. That was lacking. That was brought out at the Beaudoin-Edwards committee by the experts. It was not the Constitution. It was the lack of flexibility and the lack of public participation. As well, over and over again we were reminded that the Meech Lake package was presented as a fait accompli, take it or leave it, and that no changes would be permitted regardless of the level of public outcry.
I remind the House, it was a new amending formula that was used; unanimity or nothing, when they could have probably passed all of it, except for the Supreme Court, with the seven and fifty. Despite this clear message, and despite the weight of the evidence, the committee did not even have a chance to report before the Prime Minister decided to put his own approach to the public process.
We could have sat last week or this week and finished it. I do not think we can even sit next week unless we agree to sit as a committee to finish our work because the House has not agreed to let the committees resume. We saw that earlier today in the external affairs debate concerning what had happened in Question Period.

The Address
He wants the opinion of yet another committee. He wants a special joint committee that will travel, just like we have seen the Spicer committee do, just like the Beaudoin-Edwards committee has done. Yet there is no leadership in presenting concrete proposals as to what could be done to start the process.
He wants another nine months to pass before we get any specific proposal is brought forward. That is dangerously close to the deadlines Quebec has established in the referendum. More to the point, contrary to what we had heard on the Beaudoin-Edwards committee, there is no specific commitment to involve Canadians directly in the process. Once again, they may end up as spectators.
I am sure I am not the only person in the House who senses some of the same back to the wall, roll of the dice tactics that we saw between 1987 and 1990.1 do not think we need another joint committee in the fall.
I was pleased this morning to hear the new minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs outline the four stages he saw the government taking. He said we would await the reports of Spicer and Beaudoin. Then proposals would be formed by the government, and a joint committee would travel across Canada on those proposals and then it would go to the legislators.
The main thing that was brought before us is that the public wants to know that there is flexibility at all stages and in particular, at that last stage once the proposals have come back from that joint committee and before they go to the premiers, they want to know if they have any public input on that proposal.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, this is where the government has failed. It is waiting until next February to say to the public: "You may have a couple of months and that is going to be it, because Quebec is going to make its mind up one way or another". Again our back is to the wall.
Why are we not starting it now? Why are we not discussing a specific proposal over the summer? What would I put in that proposal? It does not take imagination. Most Canadians know what is in there. My leader gave an outline the other day of what his proposal should be.
First and foremost we should define what Canada is supposed to be for all Canadians. Second, I think we could go to the fact that we probably have to have a
human rights code in our Constitution because there are some who do not feel that all people are equal before the law, so we have to define it. I am one of those who feels that we should be big enough to have all people equal before the law. But that is another thing.
Spending power is a grave concern to the provinces. Why are we not talking about it? We have not talked about it since Meech failed. Why are we not talking?
Some witnesses said: "start talking". Do two stages. Start talking about what we can present to Quebec and then bring Quebec back to the table. We heard that from Mr. Pennicott in the Yukon. We heard it from other witnesses.
We also need to look at the distribution of powers. The Prime Minister mentions in the Speech from the Throne educational standards across Canada. Is he opening the way to talk about division of powers? Well, if he is, why are we not talking about it now, publicly, to see if there is not a need for a uniform standard in nine provinces of Canada of an education system respecting at all times the rights of Quebecers to their education system.
What about the aboriginal people? I have been in and out of this Chamber, by election, a number of times. It is more than time to start recognizing that they have certain rights that are inherent by virtue of having been in Canada before we came here. It is time for us, as Canadians, as politicians to put it out. We have all summer to talk about it. We have all of June. I do not see why we have to go by deadlines, particularly when it is so important to Canada that we stay together.
I could talk about the Senate. They have a majority. They appointed a majority over there. Change the Senate with your majority. Let us get down to work.
This week I was pleased to hear the member for South Shore talk about the concerns of Nova Scotians. It was a first. I was pleased and I agreed with everything he said. I would hope that if it came to a vote that he would vote with me or I would vote with him. For once in my life in Parliament we would have the same concerns for an area. This Parliament is outdated and it is a waste of effort sometimes. No wonder we are not respected by an awful lot of Canadians for not being able to sit down and tackle it.
May 16, 1991

The last thing I want to say, because my time is going, is on the economy and the competitiveness that was talked about. It was with a mixture of anger and disbelief that I read the pat on the back the government gave itself on the economy and the competitiveness in the Speech from the Throne. I am sure that the 1.4 million Canadians who are currently out of work because of the government's made-in-Canada recession had a similar response.
This government has systematically wrecked our economy and undermined our competitiveness with every decision it has taken in the past three years.
The truckers in Ontario today are a prime example. We have no VIA Rail. We have no railroad and it is doing away with the trucks. We cannot be competitive because of what? The government has jacked up interest rates to a point where there is an unprecedented spread between Canadian rates and those of our chief trading partner, the United States. There is 4 percentage points. It is forcing our businesses to pay more for capital than their chief competitors south of the border and undermining our competitive position.
It has pegged the Canadian dollar at an artificially high level in American dollars. For the year to date, it has averaged 85.7 cents U.S. This is a break with our tradition of letting it float to whatever value is justified by the realities of the Canadian economy.
This has discouraged our exports into the American markets and undermined our competitiveness. I can speak for an area that has fish and because of our interest rates and our high Canadian dollar, it is expensive to send into the U.S.
In passing, I would like to say that if it ever should come out that there was an agreement between this government and the United States under the free trade agreement to prop up the Canadian dollar to make it that high, I would hope that there would not be a Canada, if there are any Canadians left by the time this government is through with Canada, who would ever vote for them again.
It has implemented an offensive new tax, the GST. That is devastating our border communities. Even before the tax was brought into effect this year, the government knew that the GST would raise the price of Canadian goods and services an average of 3.8 per cent over those being sold in the United States.
The Address
The government also knew that the cross-border shopping trips would increase by 2 million per year, solely as a result of the GST.
Remember that 80 per cent of the Canadian population lives within only 200 miles of the American border, easy driving distance. I simply cannot understand why the government went ahead with a tax that so severely undermines our competitiveness. On that only, we hear from them that we need to have production costs that are equal to the United States.
When this government puts our interest rates at the same level as the United States, when our dollar is not pegged as it should be today for our exports, and when our taxes, GST or our personal taxes are at the same level as the United States, then maybe the costs of production in Canada might be able to come down to the same level as in the United States, and we might stop blaming the Canadian labour people for what this government has achieved in one final swoop with its economic policies.
I tell you, it may be hurting somebody over there, but he will have a chance to ask a question if he wants.
I cannot put the blame on people for this government's free trade agreement, a free trade agreement that it now wants to expand to include Mexico, where there are even cheaper production costs when we cannot compete with the United States under it because of the economic policies of this minister.
I can only say that Canada is a great country. If the people over there are hurting a little bit, maybe they should start to influence their government. Maybe if they influenced their government and spoke up in their caucus, we would not have the high interests rates that we have had that created this recession. We would have our exports going fairly into the United States. We cannot even finish our fish because the policy of this government on fish has been three ministers in less than two-and-a-half years. How can you have any polity for fish when you have a new minister every nine months. Heavens, if they created anything in the nine months I would be happy, but they have not created anything. They had to be replaced.
I am looking forward to seeing this new minister, because he has, I am sure, long experience and has been a minister of fisheries in the past. They have resurrected

May 16, 1991
The Address
the minister and I hope that by his resurrection he will have a new policy.
I do think that unless there are backbenchers who in caucus will start to talk about their economic needs in their regions, we will not have anything left. Certainly the Canadian public, the polls, everybody is telling them to change their economic outlook in Canada and let us begin to prosper.
We do not need to see truckers having their jobs done away with across the country. We do not have any rail. We are not going to have any trucks in the east. I do not know what we are going to have at the end of it. I can certainly say that at the rate this government is going, we are not going to have much.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do take exception to a number of things the member has stated, but there is one thing on which we do agree, and that is that we do have a great country.
Obviously, to maintain a great country, you have to respond to changes that the modem world is demanding. I know the hon. member takes exception to that because change is always difficult. The difficulty in our position is simply that we are a government that takes its responsibilities seriously and if to meet the demands of the world marketplace we have to change, we are going to change. It is never easy. The result of that is simply that we are low in the polls, because change is never easy.
Again, the hon. member is going through that old bag of Liberal philosophy, the one they have tagged and carried along with them since 1987-88.
Every sparrow that falls they blame on this government and our trade agreement. What she chooses to ignore is simply this. The last figures coming out of Canada-U.S. trade indicates that we are winning, that we have a $16 billion to $17 billion trade surplus. It means despite what the member states, we are doing a number of things right.
The hon. member wants to concentrate on the negative, and that is fine, but let us take a look at the big picture. In Canada, the trade agreement is working to our benefit. If you want to look at isolated statistics in relation to unemployment, unemployment in the United
States is 10 times higher than ours. Do they blame that on the trade agreement with Canada? Of course not.
There are other factors involved there, mainly a downturn in the western economy. We are part of that western economy. We cannot ignore that. We cannot bury our heads in the sand.
The hon. member also moved into an area of particular concern to me. It is the relation to cross-border shopping. No one ignores the fact that we have a problem in that regard. Again, in a province as small as the one that 1 represent, the province of New Brunswick, in the big picture we do very well.
The member again chooses to ignore that statistic. The province of New Brunswick has a $600 million trade surplus with the state of Maine despite all the crossborder shopping that takes place.
She chooses to ignore that very figure and takes a look at the Canadian dollar. The Canadian dollar is simply a reflection of the strength of the Canadian economy. Any economist will tell you that.
It simply means that the other countries of the world have confidence in us as a nation. If they did not believe in us, we would have a 50 cent dollar. That is the difference between our philosophy and their philosophy. For years, they wanted to prop themselves up with a weak Canadian dollar.
In the long term, that is not the answer. The longterm answer is we have to be competitive. If we are competitive and we are doing the things that are necessary to maintain a strong and healthy Canadian economy, the result is you are going to have a strong Canadian dollar.
I, for one, if I was in the exporting business, would love to have a weak Canadian dollar, but there is a price that is paid for that, a price that you pay for a weak dollar. The hon. member lorows very well what it is, because she has an understanding of economics which is sometimes clouded by the political party that she represents.
We are doing very well in the international marketplace, and I do not want the member to distort the big picture. She is very effective at distorting the big picture when she chooses to do so, although on an individual basis she starts out very well.
May 16, 1991

I think she is reflecting her own sense of where she is and what is going on. When she gets into the big black cloud that sort of looms over her party, she falls into that same trap that they have entrapped themselves in, not going beyond that.
We, as a party, will go beyond that. We will make the tough decisions that are going to be good for all Canadians in the long haul.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say to the hon. member that I do not think I distort any facts.
We can all have our party policies, and whatever. What I was bringing out was that there are production costs that this government has control over and has had control over. One is the interest rate. One is the Canadian dollar and one is certainly the level of taxes.
The GST could not have come at a worse time. I think it was in The Financial Times or somebody in the paper the other day who said: "If the free trade agreement was good policy, it was the wrong time, and if the GST is supposed to be so good, why was it brought in at the wrong time as well?"
I can say that I am glad that the GST is going to pay off the deficit. I ask only: What has the government done with all the money that it has collected since January? It still has not introduced a bill since the budget came out in February showing that it is going to put on the deficit. Is it that strapped that it has to keep going with the GST to run the government? It could make some other decisions like believe the commissions that it has set up for millions of dollars, believe what people are saying to those commissions and start looking at the problem right now of keeping Canada together so we can get down to the basics of the economy.
The only other thing I would say is, yes, Canada is an exporter. I have known that all my life. Therefore, we need a low dollar right now in order to get our exports up and to get the economy going. If the member does not understand that, I do not know what else I can say.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to participate today in the throne speech debate. This new session of Parliament signals a new beginning, a new determination by this government to take the steps necessary to help Canada and all Canadians to face the challenges of the future.
There are some disturbing realities that face us as a nation, and as citizens of the world, in this first year of the last decade of the last century of this millennium. The list is daunting; the future of Canada as a confederation, the state of the environment, the ability of the economy to continue to generate growth and jobs, the plight of children in poverty. And what makes many of these realities so disturbing is that they in themselves compromise our ability to deal with the challenges and the changes that are confronting us.
We are constantly assailed with mountains of news and information, and yet 40 per cent of Canadians cannot read a daily newspaper. We worry about our farmers
having too much product and not enough markets, while untold millions of people are facing starvation in places like Iraq, Bangladesh, Ethiopia and Sudan. We worry about the quality of the education that our children are receiving, while the job market is changing so fast that some of the professions they are training for will have disappeared by the time they are out of school.
There is an old adage that the only constant in the world is change. It sounds trite, but its truth is all around for us to see. And it is also true that those who know how to deal with and adapt to change will ride the crest of the wave of history, and those who do not will be swept along by the tide against their wills. We have no choice but to adapt to change, but we do have a choice about whether we make it work for us.
What this means is that change should not be feared, it should be welcomed. If we can make it work for us instead of against us, we can make Canada a more prosperous, more progressive, and more unified country. It is not so much the changes that we make, but the way that we make them, that give us the opportunities to move ahead.
You will remember that one of the themes of the last federal election campaign was about managing change. Candidates of both the Progressive Conservative and the Liberal parties used the phrase. It was a favourite of the pollsters for quite a while. Personally, it always made me think of a child putting his or her quarters and dimes into a piggy bank. However ridiculous the phrase, there is an important concept behind it. People are quite rightly afraid of change, or at least the implications of change, but they are also realistic about the fact that it is inevitable and part of life.
They know that promises of some to stop change, or to turn the clock back to a simpler time, are just insulting to their intelligence. Tb quote Derek Burney, our Ambassador to the United States, "Stop the world, I want to get off", may be a comforting slogan for some, but it does not offer a very promising trip.
At the same time, we must recognize that our society has a finite capacity to accept radical change. Conservatism is a trait deeply ingrained in Canadians. We are suspicious about bold new policies that promise to solve all of our problems overnight. We are especially suspicious of bold new policies offered up by governments, and rightly so. We remember the National Energy Program and Allan MacEachen's 1982 budget. We know
May 16, 1991

that they are still paying for those mistakes, in lost economic opportunities and higher debt servicing costs.
The signs of too much change, too fast, can be disturbing. We see it in the rise in unemployment and plant closings, and in lost international markets for our products. We also see it in growing racial intolerance in our cities, and in the rising violence against women and children. It is reflected in questions about our immigration policies, about the size and effect of the national debt, about the ability of the Canadian confederation to cope with the aspirations of Quebec and the west.
Therefore, we must recognize the finite capacity of the Canadian economy and society to adapt to change. It is the duty of the government and of this Etouse to propose and consider the means to increase our capacity to adapt to change. In this way we can ensure that change becomes an accepted part of life, not something to be feared.
This means that all Canadians should become more aware of the challenges that we are all facing together, and more aware of our collective strengths and skills. This means that we must be more tolerant of each other, less afraid of each other, less violent toward each other. A change in peoples' attitudes toward other languages, other cultures and other races will not happen overnight, but there are important steps that can be taken soon, that will contribute to changed attitudes.
We can take steps toward making the workforce more skilled and flexible and therefore more secure and prosperous. We can take steps toward developing a literate and numerate population more receptive to new ideas. We can take steps toward making sure that our children are healthy, well nourished and well cared for and therefore ready to embrace the challenges that the next century holds in store for them.
Canadians want to make sure that they can individually and collectively adjust to the changes that they are facing. They want to be able to adjust, they want to be able to take advantage of new opportunities. In other words, they may be conservative, but they are also progressive.
The Address
What is even more important than the decisions we make as a government and as a Parliament is how we make them. People will no longer accept decisions made behind closed doors. They want to be part of the decision-making process. The process must be open, consultative and co-operative; it must rise above petty partisanship or narrow self-interest.
It must also be realistic and workable. It cannot be possible for the entire process to be derailed by a single individual or group with their own agenda. It is far easier to say no and to ignore the consequences than it is to participate in the process that finds the way to say yes.
The challenge we face is to find a way to get more people involved in the process, to make more people involved in the quest to find a solution acceptable to as broad a spectrum as possible, to make our democratic system work better.
Therefore, I see the challenge that we face in this session of Parliament as threefold. First, we must recognize the real limits of the capacity of Canada and Canadians to deal with change. Second, we must pursue policies that will work to expand these limits. Third, we must pursue these policies in a more open and more democratic way.
What does this mean in practical terms? Let me talk about one of the most pressing and tragic issues facing Canada today, one that concerns me greatly.
At least one in every ten women in Canada is battered by her male partner. A million women in Canada are battered weekly. Half of all women murdered each year die at the hands of their partners. The prevalence of such violence in Canada is nothing less than shocking. Some say that this violence is increasing as the advances made by women in society triggers a backlash, while others claim that the abuse women suffer at the hands of men is simply part of the uneven distribution of power in society.
The challenge for everyone involved in the issue is to find a way of preventing the violence from occurring in the first place, by changing deep-seated attitudes. We in this House can change laws in a matter of months but attitudes, values and behaviour can take far longer to change.

Mr. Speaker, in Canada, the trucking industry employs approximately 500,000 Canadians. It generates about 12 billion dollars annually, and is an important industry in our country.
Last Friday, I was very disappointed to learn that Glengarry Transport, better known as GTL in our region, went bankrupt. About 1,794 employees were left without a job. No more jobs in an industry and in a community that certainly needed good jobs like the ones GTL provided.
Mr. Speaker, the jobs at GTL were certainly good jobs for my constituents, but they were more than that. In my town, when we saw the name "Glengarry" or "GTL" painted in yellow on the trucks, all the residents of Glengarry were rightfully proud. GTL was founded in 1948 by Mr. Lefebvre and today, or at least until last Friday, the company was still operated by his sons. Until 1988, the company had never lost any money. Forty consecutive years of profit. All of a sudden, in 1988, there was deregulation and since then, losses.

It is more than a coincidence, 40 years of regulations, 40 years of profits; three years of deregulation, three years of huge losses at GTL.

If members opposite or others think this situation might be exclusive to GTL, that there might have been some mismanagement, they should look further. They should look, for example, at Kingsway Transport, a leading transport company in Canada, which is now for sale. The owners of Federal Industries want to get rid of the business because it is losing money.
If people think this situation is exclusive to these two large companies, they should go outside today and see the, independent truckers who, are also facing the same problems.
On April 29,1 wrote to the new Minister of Transport asking for his help not only for GTL, but also for all the workers in the Canadian transport industry.
Last week, on Thursday I had the honor of meeting with the Minister of State (Transport) and, accompanied by Mr. Gilles Lefebvre from GTL (Transport), I made representations to him. I told him why GTL was at its very end. At that time, I had no idea the company would go bankrupt 24 hours later.
So, Mr. Speaker, today we are in the House and the government must do whatever it can to help the transport industry in general, but particularly the GTL workers who have lost their jobs. At this very minute, I have just been told that all attempts to reorganize the company have failed. So, it is sure and final now, and early today, GTL had to shut down.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of TVansport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his notice of the question and the concern that he has so eloquently expressed on behalf of his constituents.
I think the member would like me to set the record straight. This government has been listening to the truckers. Last year the former Minister of Transport initiated dialogue with the truckers. There is not now nor has there ever been any disagreement about the fact that truckers are facing difficult times. The minister has been

most sympathetic about the difficulties the truckers are facing.
What we have had to say though is that there is no quick fix here. As the minister has said in the House and in the meetings he has held is that he is willing to work with the truckers.
The minister has shown his good faith. This morning he met for an hour and a half with the truckers who are parked on Wellington Street and who have been on Parliament Hill this week. The minister has arranged a further meeting today between the truckers and his officials. He met yesterday afternoon with the wives of the truckers. He met the day before with the coalition, and he is scheduled next week to meet with the Canadian Trucking Association.
There is another point that must be made here, which is to point out the very large provincial involvement in this issue. I am not pointing fingers, I am really stating facts. The provincial fuel tax question, particularly in Ontario, must be recognized.
Last, I want to make it clear that we have been working very hard for many weeks and months. We will continue to work hard with all the parties; the truckers, our provincial colleagues, the unions and shippers. I hope we made it clear that we are involved and will stay involved.

Mr. Speaker, this is a follow-up to my question to the Prime Minister on Tuesday concerning the Air-India disaster.
Last Friday, Inderjit Singh Reyat was convicted of manslaughter in the 1985 bombing which took place at Narita airport in Japan. That particular incident and the Air-India disaster took place 54 minutes apart.
In the Air-India disaster on June 23, 1985, 329 people were killed, 280 of whom were Canadians. There were 80 children on board. It was the biggest mass murder in Canadian history.
Over the course of the last six years I have pressed this government for a royal commission of inquiry into this particular disaster. The government has continued to come up with excuses one after another.
Adjournment Debate
One of the excuses it continued to use was that there were criminal proceedings ongoing into the related Narita bombing. Those criminal proceedings are now over. A conviction has been secured.
Another excuse this government has been giving is that there were civil proceedings ongoing. The families of the victims have sued Air-India, the Government of Canada and others. Those civil proceedings are all settled and the Government of Canada contributed to the settlement which would indicate some type of responsibility on its part.
The criminal investigation into the Air-India disaster has reached a dead end. The Government of Canada and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police know who did it, yet they do not have the evidence in order to convict the person or persons who committed this horrendous and hideous crime.
A royal commission of inquiry is absolutely essential in order to assist in the criminal investigation. It is also essential in order to determine the role that the Government of Canada played in this particular matter, the role of the security intelligence service and the role of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
There have been allegations that the Government of Canada received advance warning before the bomb went off on June 23, 1985. We know about erased tapes. We know about false affidavits. We know about CSIS bungling. We know about RCMP bungling. Yet the government refuses a royal commission of inquiry.
I suspect it is because of the embarrassment that a royal commission of inquiry will cause. I would like to remind the House in closing that when it came to the conduct of Sinclair Stevens-we all remember Sinclair Stevens, who was a former Conservative cabinet minister-the government was quick to call a royal commission of inquiry.
It cost the taxpayers of Canada $5 million in order to conduct that inquiry. The taxpayers of Canada paid Mr. Stevens' legal fees in the amount of $500,000. Now we are dealing with the biggest mass murder ever in history of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the member for his question because it is one that has been of interest to me and to my constituents as well.
Mr. Speaker, together with all Canadians, I share the hon. member's desire to find satisfactory answers to the terrible tragedy which occurred off the coast of Ireland in the summer of 1985.
The continuation of the police investigation into this matter is the appropriate response and one which requires our full support. I can assure the member that the downing of the Air-India flight 182 on June 23, 1985 is still under active investigation by the RCMP and all investigative leads are being vigorously pursued.
I point, for example, to plans now being made to send four RCMP investigators, an RCMP laboratory expert and a Transportation Safety Board of Canada expert to the Air-India crash site in the North Atlantic, 110 miles off Cork, Ireland.
This significant undertaking will commence in early July and will take up to one month to complete. The purpose of this endeavour is to recover certain wreckage which will further the ongoing RCMP investigation.
In the summer of 1989, an RCMP expedition successfully raised pieces from the plane's debris from the ocean floor. This summer, the RCMP team will work at the crash site from a vessel fitted with a remote operated vehicle capable of working in 5,000 metres of water. The wreckage of the downed Air-India aircraft is located at a depth of about 2,000 metres.
Any items of wreckage recovered will be shipped back to Canada for detailed forensic examination and analysis. The recovery operation planned for this summer is but one step in a continuing RCMP investigation.
In my view, it is essential that the RCMP continue in an unimpeded fashion its exploration of all possible avenues of this most important investigation.
