Mr. Speaker, when my great grandparents came to Canada in 1884, they built their own home in Toronto on Broadview Avenue, across from Riverdale Park. They were homeowners. My grandparents after them were homeowners.
My parents were homeowners and when I was growing up, like you, Mr. Speaker, I just assumed that one day I too would be a homeowner.
Today, fortunately, my wife and I are homeowners. Home ownership is the cornerstone of this country. It is the dream of most Canadians. Fortunately, in Canada, we have one of the highest rates of home ownership in the world; some 62 per cent of Canadian households are home owners.
But today, young Canadians are asking themselves if they will ever having the opportunity to be homeowners. The Prime Minister alluded to that yesterday when he said that our children may be the first generation of Canadians to be worse off than their parents.
That is why we have to break down some of the barriers to home ownership. What are those barriers? We have barriers like high housing prices; we have zoning that discourages the construction of affordable housing; we have high interest rates for mortgages; we have a lack of confidence in our future employment, and we have high down payments.
A lot of those things we cannot do anything about, but we can do something about the high down payments, because presently, if you have a down payment of 25 per cent or more there is no problem. You can get a mortgage, no problem at all. If you have a down payment somewhere between 10 per cent and 25 per cent, then the mortgage lender requires mortgage insurance and that is the only way that you could get a mortgage. If you have a down payment of less than 10 per cent, no way, you cannot get mortgage insurance, you cannot get a mortgage at all.
The government housing agency, CMHC, has estimated however that if we dropped homeowner downpayments to 5 per cent, with a 95 per cent mortgage insurance, we could ensure that up to 200,000 additional households across this country could become home owners.
Why do we not do that? When interest rates were going up, I was told that would to stimulate demand and send the wrong message. But now, as you know, interest rates are going down. In fact, in addition to that we have double digit unemployment, 15.5 per cent more unemployment in the construction trades than we had a year ago, prices are down, and surely now it is an ideal time to
May 16, 1991

lower down payments and allow more people to be home owners.
The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have often asked the opposition for its ideas as to how to create jobs, but at the same time not increase the deficit and the national debt. Well, this will do it.
At the same time as increasing home ownership and increasing employment, however, it is also going to help young Canadians to realize their dream of home ownership.
My Progressive Conservative Party wants to encourage home ownership. What does your Progressive Conservative Party want to do, Mr. Minister?

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank, on behalf of the Minister for Housing, my colleague Alan Redway for his suggestion about creating jobs in construction by lowering the down payment on a home to 5 per cent.

Canada is a nation of homeowners. In fact, Canadians enjoy one of the highest rates of home ownership in the world, about 62 per cent over all.

The best way to create jobs and help people become homeowners is to build a strong economy. To that end, we need low interest rates and moderate inflation. If we achieve that, business and consumers will regain confidence in the economy.
That is the approach this government has chosen. Interest rates have gone down five points in the last eleven months, and inflation is stable.

Business confidence is rising. There is good news for the residential construction industry and future home buyers. Yesterday, the Canadian Real Estate Association reported sales of existing housing across the country soared over 66 per cent since this time last year.
In my riding of Manicouagan, several millions of dollars in loans were insured by CMHC in 1990.
The opportunity to own a home is an important value in Canada. Home ownership encourages stable commu-
Adjoumment Debate
nities and helps individuals and families build equity for the future.

Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is presently considering various ways to help Canadians buy their own homes. One way would be a mortgage insurance for people who can only afford a down payment of 5 per cent. This insurance would be guaranteed by the government.

CMHC studies estimate that by reducing down payments to 5 per cent, it would allow up to 200,000 Canadian renters a reasonable opportunity for home ownership. Of these, there could some 10,000 potential first-time homeowners in the first year.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, we want to help home buyers, and this is my answer to the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, I asked a question of the Minister of Immigration and it bears repeating. It concerns the Al-Mashat case. I asked very simply:
Why did this former mouthpiece for Saddam Hussein get preferential treatment at the expense of ordinary people waiting patiently? Why was he allowed to jump the queue?
The minister did not answer.
Canadians know that there are rules and that for every rule, there is an exception. Canadians also know that ministers are the custodians of the public trust and they are expected to implement and respect the rules and to explain and justify the exceptions.
Let us look at this case. On Wednesday, February 27, External Affairs is advised that Mr. Al-Mashat wishes to defect. The next day, Thursday, the defector committee meets and rejects his application as a defector. The next day, Friday, the Canadian Security and Intelligence Service conducts its first inquiries. Canadians are asked to believe that the defector committee did not think it important enough to advise the minister that Al-Mashat had been rejected.
May 16, 1991

Adjournment Debate
Canadians are asked to believe that CSIS found the former ambassador not to be a valuable source of intelligence. Canadians are asked to believe that no one at CSIS thought it important enough to advise the minister.
On Tuesday, March 5, the Al-Mashats are interviewed. Who interviewed them? Who suggested to them that they apply as retirees, a class that the minister of immigration had announced was being phased out and which, in fact, will disappear June 30.
Canadians are asked to believe that officials in Vienna did not think this man important enough to advise our ambassador in Vienna.
On Thursday, March 7, the Al-Mashats had their second interview and are given provisional acceptance, two days after their first interview.
On March 8, a memorandum is sent to the Secretary of State for External Affairs explaining the situation. Canadians are asked to believe that the memo was not brought to the external affairs minister's attention. On March 11, senior immigration officials are so concerned that they call external affairs and Mr. Paul Tellier, Clerk of the Privy Council, to insist that the application not be fast-tracked. Canadians are asked to believe that these senior officials did not, despite their concern, alert their own minister.
March 28, landed immigrant status is granted to the Al-Mashats, 28 days from start to finish, including interviews, medical clearances and CSIS security checks for a man that CSIS found not to be a valued source of intelligence. That process for ordinary people takes, at best, 12 to 18 months and, more usually, two to three
years. But for him, 28 days and no minister knows about it.
I ask again: Why was this man given preferential treatment? Canadians have the right to know.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to this question, the reason why Dr. Al-Mashat's immigration application was processed quickly has already been addressed in a report by the Deputy Ministers of Employment and Immigration and External Affairs. This report, which was made public on May 14, 1991, is based on the findings of an extensive inquiry into the circumstances under which Dr. Al-Ma-shat was granted admission to Canada.
This afternoon, the Secretary of State for External Affairs confirmed on several occasions the willingness of ministers to appear before a parliamentary committee together with officials concerned to respond to questions on this matter. The Minister of Employment and Immigration has stated in the House that there is no need to table any document related to Dr. Al-Mashat's admission to Canada. The report by the Deputy Ministers of Employment and Immigration and External Affairs released on May 14, 1991, clearly outline the circumstances of Dr. Al-Mashat's case.
This government has acted openly and responsibly on this issue, and will continue to do so.
